turns.en: Grandad, what year were you born? Where did you live when you were little?

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 一九五八年，在北京的一条胡同里生的。那时候一个院子住了五户人家，厨房大家合用，一家一个煤炉。早上家家户户生炉子，整条胡同都是烟。买米要粮票，买肉要肉票，一个月吃上一顿红烧肉，就像过年。
turns.pinyin: yī jiǔ wǔ bā nián, zài Běijīng de yī tiáo hútòng lǐ shēng de. nàshíhou yī gè yuànzi zhù le wǔ hù rénjiā, chúfáng dàjiā héyòng, yī jiā yī gè méilú. zǎoshang jiājiāhùhù shēnglúzi, zhěng tiáo hútòng dōu shì yān. mǎi mǐ yào liángpiào, mǎi ròu yào ròupiào, yī gè yuè chīshàng yī dùn hóng shāo ròu, jiù xiàng guònián.
turns.en: 1958. I was born in a hutong in Beijing. Back then there were five households in one courtyard. Everyone shared the kitchen, one coal stove per family. In the morning every household lit its stove and the whole hutong filled with smoke. You needed grain coupons for rice and meat coupons for meat. Braised pork once a month was like New Year.

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 听起来很苦。
turns.pinyin: tīngqilai hěn kǔ.
turns.en: It sounds hard.

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 苦是苦，可是热闹。夏天晚上，大家把竹椅子搬到胡同里乘凉，大人聊天，小孩子听故事。现在回想起来，那是我最开心的时候。
turns.pinyin: kǔ shì kǔ, kěshì rènao. xiàtiān wǎnshang, dàjiā bǎ zhúyǐzi bān dào hútòng lǐ chéngliáng, dàren liáotiān, xiǎo háizi tīng gùshi. xiànzài huíxiǎngqǐlái, nà shì wǒ zuì kāixīn de shíhou.
turns.en: Hard, yes, but lively. On summer evenings everyone carried bamboo chairs out into the hutong to sit in the cool. The grown-ups chatted and the children listened to stories. Looking back now, those were my happiest days.

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 你每次都说以前好。可是那时候家里连个卫生间都没有，天天早上倒马桶，你忘了？
turns.pinyin: nǐ měi cì dōu shuō yǐqián hǎo. kěshì nàshíhou jiā lǐ lián gè wèishēngjiān dōu méiyǒu, tiān tiān zǎoshang dào mǎtǒng, nǐ wàng le?
turns.en: You always say things were better before. But back then there wasn't even a toilet in the house. Emptying the chamber pot every morning, have you forgotten?

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 没忘。所以说，日子是越过越好了，就是人和人越来越远了。
turns.pinyin: méi wàng. suǒyǐ shuō, rìzi shì yuè guò yuè hǎole, jiùshì rénhérén yuèláiyuè yuǎn le.
turns.en: I haven't. Which is why I say life keeps getting better; it's just that people keep getting further apart.

turns.name: 朵朵
turns.hanzi: 爷爷，奶奶说您在纺织厂工作过？
turns.pinyin: yéye, nǎinai shuō nín zài fǎngzhīchǎng gōngzuò guo?
turns.en: Grandad, Grandma says you worked in a textile mill?

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 二十岁进厂，三班倒，一干就是二十二年。后来厂子不行了，我四十二岁那年下岗了。那一年，真是天塌下来了。
turns.pinyin: èr shí suì jìn chǎng, sānbāndǎo, yī gàn jiùshì èr shí èr nián. hòulái chǎngzi bùxíng le, wǒ sì shí èr suì nànián xiàgǎng le. nà yī nián, zhēnshi tiāntāxiàlái le.
turns.en: I went into the mill at twenty, three shifts round the clock, and stayed twenty-two years. Then the mill went under, and I was laid off the year I turned forty-two. That year, it really felt like the sky had fallen in.

turns.name: 陈明
turns.hanzi: 那年我才六岁。我记得妈妈天天晚上在灯下织毛衣，第二天爸爸拿到路边去卖。
turns.pinyin: nànián wǒ cái liù suì. wǒ jìde māma tiān tiān wǎnshang zài dēng xià zhī máoyī, dì èr tiān bàba ná dào lù biān qù mài.
turns.en: I was only six. I remember Mum knitting under the lamp every night, and the next day Dad would take the jumpers out to sell by the road.

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 后来我在菜场摆过摊，在超市当过收银员，什么都做过。现在想想，也不知道那时候哪来的力气。
turns.pinyin: hòulái wǒ zài càichǎng bǎi guo tān, zài chāoshì dāng guo shōuyínyuán, shénme dōu zuò guo. xiànzài xiǎng xiang, yě bù zhīdào nàshíhou nǎ lái de lìqi.
turns.en: After that I ran a stall at the market, worked on a supermarket till, did everything. Thinking about it now, I don't know where I found the strength.

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 陈明，你小时候觉得爸爸辛苦吗？
turns.pinyin: Chénmíng, nǐ xiǎoshíhou juéde bàba xīnkǔ ma?
turns.en: Chen Ming, when you were little, did you realise how hard it was for your dad?

turns.name: 陈明
turns.hanzi: 那时候不懂。等我自己当了父亲，天天为朵朵上学的事发愁，才明白他当年吃了多少苦。
turns.pinyin: nàshíhou bù dǒng. děng wǒ zìjǐ dāng le fùqīn, tiān tiān wèi Duǒduo shàng xué de shì fāchóu, cái míngbai tā dāngnián chī le duōshǎo kǔ.
turns.en: Not back then. Only once I was a father myself, worrying about Duoduo's schooling every day, did I understand how much he went through.

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 我们这代人，什么都缺，就是不缺时间。他们这代人，什么都不缺，就是缺时间。朵朵这代人呢……我就看不懂了。
turns.pinyin: wǒmen zhè dài rén, shénme dōu quē, jiùshì bù quē shíjiān. tāmen zhè dài rén, shénme dōu bù quē, jiùshì quē shíjiān. Duǒduo zhè dài rén ne wǒ jiù kàn bu dǒng le.
turns.en: My generation went without everything, except time. His generation has everything, except time. As for Duoduo's generation... I can't make them out at all.

turns.name: 朵朵
turns.hanzi: 爷爷，这句话，我要写在海报的最上面。
turns.pinyin: yéye, zhè jù huà, wǒ yào xiě zài hǎibào de zuì shàng miàn.
turns.en: Grandad, I'm going to put that right at the top of my poster.

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 写在最上面？那要写得好看点儿。好了，今天就讲到这里，老照片明天再给你找。
turns.pinyin: xiě zài zuì shàng miàn? nà yào xiě de hǎokàn diǎnr. hǎole, jīntiān jiù jiǎng dào zhè lǐ, lǎozhàopiàn míngtiān zài gěi nǐ zhǎo.
turns.en: Right at the top? Then write it nicely. Right, that's enough for today. I'll find you the old photographs tomorrow.

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 都去洗手。下个礼拜三端午节，我包粽子，谁也不许出去吃。
turns.pinyin: dōu qù xǐshǒu. xià gè lǐbài sān duānwǔjié, wǒ bāo zòngzi, shéi yě bùxǔ chūqu chī.
turns.en: Go and wash your hands, all of you. It's the Dragon Boat Festival next Wednesday. I'm making zongzi, and nobody's eating out.

dialogues.title: The first of the dog days

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 今天入伏了，外面三十七度。来，一人一碗绿豆汤，消消暑。朵朵，冰箱里那碗别拿，刚从外面回来就喝冰镇的，伤胃。
turns.pinyin: jīntiān rùfú le, wàimiàn sānshíqī dù. lái, yī rén yī wǎn lǜdòutāng, xiāo xiāoshǔ. Duǒduo, bīngxiāng lǐ nà wǎn bié ná, gāng cóng wàimiàn huílai jiù hē bīngzhèn de, shāng wèi.
turns.en: The dog days start today, and it's thirty-seven degrees out. Here, a bowl of mung bean soup each, to cool you down. Duoduo, leave the bowl in the fridge. Ice-cold when you've just come in is bad for your stomach.

turns.name: 小雨
turns.hanzi: 谢谢姨妈。姨父，手术做完七个星期了，腿好点儿了吗？
turns.pinyin: xièxie yímā. yífu, shǒushù zuò wán qī gè xīngqī le, tuǐ hǎo diǎnr le ma?
turns.en: Thanks, Auntie. Uncle, it's seven weeks since the operation. Are your legs any better?

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 还行。我天天给他炖骨头汤，老话说“吃什么补什么”嘛。
turns.pinyin: háixíng. wǒ tiān tiān gěi tā dùn gǔtoutāng, lǎohuà shuō chīshénmebǔshénme ma.
turns.en: He's doing all right. I make him bone soup every day. As the old saying goes, 'you are what you eat'.

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 天天骨头汤，我都快喝成骨头了！她还不让我出门，说“伤筋动骨一百天”，非让我躺满一百天不可。
turns.pinyin: tiān tiān gǔtoutāng, wǒ dōu kuài hē chéng gǔtou le! tā hái bùràng wǒ chūmén, shuō shāngjīndònggǔ yī bǎi tiān, fēi ràng wǒ tǎng mǎn yī bǎi tiān bùkě.
turns.en: Bone soup every day! I'm turning into a bone. And she won't let me out of the house. She says 'a broken bone takes a hundred days', so I've got to lie here for the full hundred.

turns.name: 小雨
turns.hanzi: 姨妈，说句实话，换了关节以后，最怕的就是一直躺着。出院的时候，医生不是说了吗？要尽早下地活动，每天做康复训练，不然关节容易僵硬。
turns.pinyin: yímā, shuōjùshíhuà, huàn le guānjié yǐhòu, zuì pà de jiùshì yīzhí tǎng zhe. chūyuàn de shíhou, yīshēng bùshì shuō le ma? yào jǐnzǎo xiàdì huódòng, měitiān zuò kāngfùxùnliàn, bùrán guānjié róngyì jiāngyìng.
turns.en: Auntie, to be honest, after a joint replacement, the worst thing you can do is stay lying down. Didn't the doctor say so when he left hospital? He should be up and moving as soon as possible, doing his rehab exercises every day. Otherwise the joints get stiff.

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 可是我在视频上看到一个专家说，这个时候一定要静养，还说骨头汤补钙，喝了骨头长得快。
turns.pinyin: kěshì wǒ zài shìpín shang kàn dào yī gè zhuānjiā shuō, zhège shíhou yīdìng yào jìngyǎng, hái shuō gǔtoutāng bǔgài, hē le gǔtou zhǎngde kuài.
turns.en: But I saw an expert in a video who said he must rest completely now, and that bone soup is full of calcium, so the bones heal faster.

turns.name: 小雨
turns.hanzi: 姨妈，您先查查这个“专家”是谁、在哪家医院。研究表明，骨头汤里的钙其实少得可怜，喝下去的大多是油。要补钙，不如喝牛奶、吃豆腐。
turns.pinyin: yímā, nín xiān chá cha zhège zhuānjiā shì shéi, zài nǎ jiā yīyuàn. yánjiūbiǎomíng, gǔtoutāng lǐ de gài qíshí shǎo de kělián, hē xiàqu de dà duō shì yóu. yào bǔgài, bùrú hē niúnǎi, chī dòufu.
turns.en: Auntie, first check who this 'expert' is and which hospital he works at. Research shows there's hardly any calcium in bone soup. Most of what you drink is fat. If he needs calcium, milk and tofu are much better.

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 听见没有？小雨说的都有根据，比你那些视频靠谱多了。
turns.pinyin: tīngjiàn méiyǒu? Xiǎoyǔ shuō de dōu yǒu gēnjù, bǐ nǐ nàxiē shìpín kàopǔ duōle.
turns.en: Hear that? Xiaoyu has something to back up what she says. She's a lot more reliable than those videos of yours.

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 好好好，我说不过你们。可是这么热的天，他在屋里还不肯开空调，说吹多了会得“空调病”。
turns.pinyin: hǎohǎo hǎo, wǒ shuō buguò nǐmen. kěshì zhème rè de tiān, tā zài wū lǐ hái bù kěn kāi kōngtiáo, shuō chuī duōle huì dé kōngtiáobìng.
turns.en: All right, all right, I can't argue with the lot of you. But in this heat he still won't turn the air conditioning on indoors. He says too much of it gives you 'air-con sickness'.

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 这一点我可没说错。三伏天吹空调，寒气进了身体，冬天就要生病。
turns.pinyin: zhèyīdiǎn wǒ kě méi shuōcuò. sānfútiān chuī kōngtiáo, hánqì jìn le shēntǐ, dōngtiān jiù yào shēngbìng.
turns.en: I'm not wrong about that. Air conditioning in the dog days lets the cold into your body, and then you fall ill in winter.

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 这倒是。所以我每年入伏都给他贴三伏贴，冬病夏治嘛。
turns.pinyin: zhè dàoshì. suǒyǐ wǒ měi nián rùfú dōu gěi tā tiē sānfútiē, dōngbìngxiàzhì ma.
turns.en: That's true enough. That's why I put the dog-day plasters on him every summer: treat winter illness in the summer.

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 叔叔，您屋里多少度啊？我刚才进去送西瓜，才站了一分钟，就出了一身汗。
turns.pinyin: shūshu, nín wū lǐ duōshǎo dù a? wǒ gāngcái jìnqu sòng xīguā, cái zhàn le yī fēnzhōng, jiù chū le yīshēn hàn.
turns.en: Uncle, how hot is it in your room? I took you some watermelon just now, and I'd only been in there a minute before I was covered in sweat.

turns.name: 小雨
turns.hanzi: 姨父，这个我真得说两句。每年夏天，医院都会收好几个中暑的老人，大多是在家里舍不得开空调的。开到二十六度左右，别对着吹，适当开窗通风，就没问题。
turns.pinyin: yífu, zhège wǒ zhēn děi shuō liǎng jù. měi nián xiàtiān, yīyuàn dōu huì shōu hǎojǐ gè zhòngshǔ de lǎorén, dà duō shì zài jiā lǐ shěbude kāi kōngtiáo de. kāi dào èrshíliù dù zuǒyòu, bié duìzhe chuī, shìdàng kāichuāng tōngfēng, jiù méiwèntí.
turns.en: Uncle, I really have to say something about this. Every summer the hospitals admit several older people with heatstroke, and most of them wouldn't run the air conditioning at home. Set it to about twenty-six, don't sit in the draught, open the windows now and then, and you'll be fine.

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 开是可以开……电费谁出？
turns.pinyin: kāi shì kěyǐ kāi diànfèi shéi chū?
turns.en: I suppose I could put it on... and who's paying for the electricity?

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 我出，我出！其实英国人也有自己的“养生”，比如“一天一个苹果，医生远离我”。不过我们从来不喝热水，我到现在还是不习惯。
turns.pinyin: wǒ chū, wǒ chū! qíshí yīngguó rén yě yǒu zìjǐ de yǎngshēng, bǐrú yī tiān yī gè píngguǒ, yīshēng yuǎn lí wǒ. bùguò wǒmen cónglái bù hē rèshuǐ, wǒ dào xiànzài háishi bù xíguàn.
turns.en: I'll pay, I'll pay! Actually, the English have their own health sayings too, like 'an apple a day keeps the doctor away'. But we never drink hot water. I'm still not used to it.

turns.name: 朵朵
turns.hanzi: 我在伦敦上学的时候，同学们冬天也喝冰水，全班只有我一个人带保温杯。
turns.pinyin: wǒ zài Lúndūn shàng xué de shíhou, tóngxué men dōngtiān yě hē bīng shuǐ, quán bān zhǐ yǒu wǒ yī gè rén dài bǎowēnbēi.
turns.en: When I was at school in London, my classmates drank iced water even in winter. I was the only one in the class with a flask.

turns.name: 小雨
turns.hanzi: 所以说，每个地方都有自己的老话，有的有道理，有的只是习惯。老话并非都是错的：早睡早起、吃饭七分饱，都有科学根据。关键是分清楚：哪些有证据，哪些只是听说。
turns.pinyin: suǒyǐ shuō, měi gè dìfang dōu yǒu zìjǐ de lǎohuà, yǒu de yǒudàoli, yǒu de zhǐ shì xíguàn. lǎohuà bìngfēi dōu shì cuò de: zǎoshuìzǎoqǐ, chīfàn qīfēnbǎo, dōu yǒu kēxué gēnjù. guānjiàn shì fēn qīngchu: nǎxiē yǒu zhèngjù, nǎxiē zhǐ shì tīngshuō.
turns.en: So every place has its old sayings. Some make sense, and some are just habit. Old sayings aren't all wrong. Early to bed and early to rise, eating till you're seventy per cent full: there's science behind those. The key is to tell the difference: what has evidence, and what's just hearsay.

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 好！从明天开始，我每天早上去公园走两圈，走完了再唱两段。
turns.pinyin: hǎo! cóng míngtiān kāishǐ, wǒ měitiān zǎoshang qù gōngyuán zǒu liǎng quān, zǒu wán le zài chàng liǎng duàn.
turns.en: Right! From tomorrow, I'll do two laps of the park every morning, and sing a couple of pieces when I'm done.

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 走可以，唱就算了，邻居还要睡觉呢！
turns.pinyin: zǒu kěyǐ, chàng jiù suànle, línjū hái yào shuìjiào ne!
turns.en: Walk by all means, but forget the singing. The neighbours are trying to sleep!

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 今天在洞里看了一上午壁画，上上下下那么多台阶，我这两个新膝盖一点儿事都没有！
turns.pinyin: jīntiān zài dòng lǐ kàn le yī shàngwǔ bìhuà, shàng shàng xià xià nàme duō táijiē, wǒ zhè liǎng gè xīn xīgài yīdiǎnr shì dōu méiyǒu!
turns.en: A whole morning looking at murals in the caves, up and down all those steps, and my two new knees didn't give me a bit of trouble!

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 还说呢，一上午你坐下来休息了八次。马克，你怎么半天不说话？
turns.pinyin: hái shuō ne, yī shàngwǔ nǐ zuòxia lái xiūxi le bā cì. Mǎkè, nǐ zěnme bàntiān bù shuōhuà?
turns.en: Listen to him. You sat down for a rest eight times this morning. Mark, why so quiet?

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 阿姨，我到现在脑子里还全是颜色。一千多年前的蓝色和绿色，到今天还那么鲜艳。
turns.pinyin: āyí, wǒ dào xiànzài nǎozi lǐ hái quán shì yánsè. yī qiān duō nián qián de lánsè hé lǜsè, dào jīntiān hái nàme xiānyàn.
turns.en: Auntie, my head's still full of colours. Blues and greens from more than a thousand years ago, still so bright today.

turns.name: 小雨
turns.hanzi: 他是设计师，一看到颜色就走不动了。
turns.pinyin: tā shì shèjìshī, yī kàn dào yánsè jiù zǒu bù dòng le.
turns.en: He's a designer. Once he sees colours, you can't move him.

turns.name: 朵朵
turns.hanzi: 马克，我问你一件事。我们班同学知道我是在伦敦出生的，老问我：英国菜是不是特别难吃？是不是天天下雨？还有人说，英国人表面上很客气，其实很冷漠，不喜欢跟外国人交朋友。
turns.pinyin: Mǎkè, wǒ wèn nǐ yī jiàn shì. wǒmen bān tóngxué zhīdào wǒ shì zài Lúndūn chūshēng de, lǎo wèn wǒ: yīngguó cài shì bùshì tèbié nánchī? shì bùshì tiān tiān xiàyǔ? hái yǒu rén shuō, yīngguó rén biǎomiànshang hěn kèqi, qíshí hěn lěngmò, bù xǐhuan gēn wàiguórén jiāopéngyou.
turns.en: Mark, can I ask you something? My classmates know I was born in London, and they keep asking me: is English food really terrible? Does it rain every day? And some of them say English people are very polite on the surface but actually cold, and don't like making friends with foreigners.

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 英国菜难吃这一条，我没法反驳。不过“英国人都很冷漠”，就有点儿以偏概全了。我来中国之前，也以为中国人都很严肃，不爱开玩笑。
turns.pinyin: yīngguó cài nánchī zhè yī tiáo, wǒ méifǎ fǎnbó. bùguò yīngguó rén dōu hěn lěngmò, jiù yǒudiǎnr yǐpiāngàiquán le. wǒ lái zhōngguó zhīqián, yě yǐwéi zhōngguó rén dōu hěn yánsù, bù ài kāiwánxiào.
turns.en: The food, I can't argue with. But 'the English are all cold' is a bit of a sweeping generalisation. Before I came to China, I thought Chinese people were all very serious and didn't joke around.

turns.name: 朵朵
turns.hanzi: 结果呢？
turns.pinyin: jiéguǒ ne?
turns.en: And?

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 结果我第一次见到你爸爸，他就开我的玩笑，到现在还没停过。
turns.pinyin: jiéguǒ wǒ dì yī cì jiàn dào nǐ bàba, tā jiù kāi wǒ de wánxiào, dào xiànzài hái méi tíng guo.
turns.en: And the first time I met your dad, he started making fun of me, and he hasn't stopped since.

turns.name: 陈明
turns.hanzi: 谁让你每次都迟到？不过说真的，这样的刻板印象，你以前还有不少吧？
turns.pinyin: shéi ràng nǐ měi cì dōu chídào? bùguò shuōzhēnde, zhèyàng de kèbǎnyìnxiàng, nǐ yǐqián hái yǒu bù shǎo ba?
turns.en: Well, who's always late? But seriously, you must have had plenty of other stereotypes like that.

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 多了。我以为中国菜都是酸酸甜甜的，因为伦敦的中餐馆都是这样。后来去了成都才知道，还有辣得让人流眼泪的。
turns.pinyin: duōle. wǒ yǐwéi zhōngguó cài dōu shì suānsuāntiántián de, yīnwèi Lúndūn de zhōngcānguǎn dōu shì zhèyàng. hòulái qù le Chéngdū cái zhīdào, hái yǒu là de ràng rén liú yǎnlèi de.
turns.en: Plenty. I thought all Chinese food was sweet and sour, because that's what it's like in London's Chinese restaurants. Then I went to Chengdu and found out there's food so spicy it makes you cry.

turns.name: 小雨
turns.hanzi: 我刚到伦敦的时候也一样，以为英国人天天喝下午茶，说话都像电影里那样。后来发现，大家早上都是一手拿咖啡，一手拿三明治，边走边吃。
turns.pinyin: wǒ gāng dào Lúndūn de shíhou yě yīyàng, yǐwéi yīngguó rén tiān tiān hē xiàwǔchá, shuōhuà dōu xiàng diànyǐng lǐ nàyàng. hòulái fāxiàn, dàjiā zǎoshang dōu shì yī shǒu ná kāfēi, yī shǒu ná sānmíngzhì, biān zǒu biān chī.
turns.en: It was the same for me when I first got to London. I thought the English had afternoon tea every day and all talked like people in films. Then I found everyone's got a coffee in one hand and a sandwich in the other in the morning, eating on the go.

turns.name: 朵朵
turns.hanzi: 那刻板印象是怎么来的呢？
turns.pinyin: nà kèbǎnyìnxiàng shì zěnme lái de ne?
turns.en: So where do stereotypes come from?

turns.name: 小雨
turns.hanzi: 大多来自电影、新闻，或者一两个人的经历。对一个地方不了解，难免会用几个简单的标签去理解它。
turns.pinyin: dà duō láizì diànyǐng, xīnwén, huòzhě yī liǎng gè rén de jīnglì. duì yī gè dìfang bù liǎojiě, nánmiǎn huì yòng jǐ gè jiǎndān de biāoqiān qù lǐjiě tā.
turns.en: Mostly from films, the news, or one or two people's experiences. When you don't know a place, you're bound to understand it through a few simple labels.

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 对我而言，旅行最大的意义，就是把这些标签一个一个撕下来。不过前提是，你得真的跟当地人聊天，而不是拍几张照片、打个卡就走。
turns.pinyin: duì wǒ éryán, lǚxíng zuì dà de yìyì, jiùshì bǎ zhèxiē biāoqiān yīgèyīgè sī xiàlai. bùguò qiántí shì, nǐ děi zhēnde gēn dāngdìrén liáotiān, ér bùshì pāi jǐ zhāng zhàopiàn, dǎ gè kǎ jiù zǒu.
turns.en: For me, the biggest point of travelling is peeling those labels off one by one. But only if you really talk to the people who live there, not just take a few photos, tick the place off and leave.

turns.name: 朵朵
turns.hanzi: 我同桌的姐姐下个月要去伦敦读研究生。她家里人都说，出去开开眼界是好事。可是她也听说了这些，有点儿紧张，还说自己的英语很一般，怕跟人聊不起来。
turns.pinyin: wǒ tóngzhuō de jiějie xià gè yuè yào qù Lúndūn dú yánjiūshēng. tā jiālirén dōu shuō, chūqu kāi kāiyǎnjiè shì hǎoshì. kěshì tā yě tīngshuō le zhèxiē, yǒudiǎnr jǐnzhāng, hái shuō zìjǐ de yīngyǔ hěn yībān, pà gēn rén liáobuqǐlái.
turns.en: The girl I sit next to has a big sister who's going to London to do a master's next month. Her family all say it'll be good for her to go and see the world. But she's heard all this too, and she's a bit nervous. She says her English isn't great, and she's scared she won't be able to hold a conversation.

turns.name: 小雨
turns.hanzi: 伦敦唐人街有一个语言交换，她可以去那儿教别人中文，顺便练练英语。我跟马克就是在那儿认识的。
turns.pinyin: Lúndūn Tángrénjiē yǒu yī gè yǔyánjiāohuàn, tā kěyǐ qù nàr jiāo biéren zhōngwén, shùnbiàn liàn liàn yīngyǔ. wǒ gēn Mǎkè jiùshì zài nàr rènshi de.
turns.en: There's a language exchange in London's Chinatown. She can go there and teach people Chinese, and practise her English while she's at it. That's where Mark and I met.

turns.name: 朵朵
turns.hanzi: 我也在！那天马克只会说“你好”。
turns.pinyin: wǒ yě zài! nà tiān Mǎkè zhǐ huì shuō nǐhǎo.
turns.en: I was there too! All Mark could say that day was 'hello'.

turns.name: 陈明
turns.hanzi: 九月七号，他正好要在那儿用中文演讲。到时候我们全家都去给他加油！
turns.pinyin: jiǔ yuè qī hào, tā zhènghǎo yào zài nàr yòng zhōngwén yǎnjiǎng. dàoshíhou wǒmen quánjiā dōu qù gěi tā jiāyóu!
turns.en: And on 7 September, as it happens, he's giving a speech there in Chinese. We'll all be there to cheer him on!

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 刚才老家的小川来电话了，说合作社有个好消息，也是个难题：一家北欧的家居品牌看了他的直播，想订五千个竹篮，明年春天在欧洲上市。
turns.pinyin: gāngcái lǎojiā de Xiǎochuān lái diànhuà le, shuō hézuòshè yǒu gè hǎo xiāoxi, yěshì gè nántí: yī jiā běi'ōu de jiājū pǐnpái kàn le tā de zhíbō, xiǎng dìng wǔ qiān gè zhúlán, míngnián chūntiān zài ōuzhōu shàngshì.
turns.en: Xiaochuan has just rung from the village. He says the co-op has good news, and a problem: a Nordic homeware brand has seen his livestreams, and wants to order five thousand baskets, to go on sale in Europe next spring.

turns.name: 朵朵
turns.hanzi: 五千个？村里的爷爷奶奶一年才编得了这么多吧！
turns.pinyin: wǔ qiān gè? cūn lǐ de yéye nǎinai yī nián cái biān de liǎo zhème duō ba!
turns.en: Five thousand? It must take the grandpas and grandmas in the village a whole year to weave that many!

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 可不是嘛，那是合作社一年的产量。而且人家有几个条件：第一，价格要比国内低三成；第二，篮子要按他们的设计改，颜色要浅，样子要简单，说是“北欧风”；第三，只贴他们的牌子，不能出现竹溪的名字。
turns.pinyin: kě bùshì ma, nà shì hézuòshè yī nián de chǎnliàng. érqiě rénjiā yǒu jǐ gè tiáojiàn: dì yī, jiàgé yào bǐ guónèi dī sānchéng; dì èr, lánzi yào àn tāmen de shèjì gǎi, yánsè yào qiǎn, yàngzi yào jiǎndān, shuō shì běi'ōu fēng; dì sān, zhǐ tiē tāmen de páizi, bù néng chūxiàn Zhúxī de míngzi.
turns.en: Exactly, that's the co-op's output for a whole year. And they have conditions. First, the price has to be thirty per cent lower than here. Second, the baskets have to be changed to their design: light colours, simple shapes, 'Nordic style', they say. Third, only their label goes on, and Zhuxi's name can't appear anywhere.

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 这不就是贴牌吗？编得再好，外国人也不知道是竹溪的老人编的。
turns.pinyin: zhè bù jiùshì tiēpái ma? biān de zài hǎo, wàiguórén yě bù zhīdào shì Zhúxī de lǎorén biān de.
turns.en: Isn't that just making them under someone else's brand? However well they're made, nobody abroad will know they were woven by old people in Zhuxi.

turns.name: 陈明
turns.hanzi: 话虽如此，贴牌也有贴牌的好处。一方面，订单稳定，村里的年轻人有活干，不用再出去打工；另一方面，也能学学人家的标准和管理。
turns.pinyin: huàsuīrúcǐ, tiēpái yě yǒu tiēpái de hǎochu. yīfāngmiàn, dìngdān wěndìng, cūn lǐ de niánqīngrén yǒu huó gàn, bùyòng zài chūqu dǎgōng; lìngyīfāngmiàn, yě néng xué xué rénjiā de biāozhǔn hé guǎnlǐ.
turns.en: That's true, but making for another brand has its advantages. On the one hand, the orders are steady, and young people in the village will have work without leaving to find it. On the other, they can learn from the brand's standards and the way it's run.

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 不可否认，这是个大机会。可是价格低三成，编一个篮子要五六个小时，老人们还挣得到钱吗？
turns.pinyin: bùkěfǒurèn, zhè shì gè dà jīhuì. kěshì jiàgé dī sānchéng, biān yī gè lánzi yào wǔ liù gè xiǎoshí, lǎorén men hái zhèng dedào qián ma?
turns.en: There's no denying it's a big opportunity. But at thirty per cent less, when a basket takes five or six hours to weave, will the old weavers still earn anything?

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 这正是小川担心的。人家一开口就压价。现在一个篮子卖一百多块，按他们的价格，一个人一天也就挣几十块钱。
turns.pinyin: zhè zhèngshì Xiǎochuān dānxīn de. rénjiā yī kāikǒu jiù yājià. xiànzài yī gè lánzi mài yī bǎi duō kuài, àn tāmen de jiàgé, yī gè rén yī tiān yě jiù zhèng jǐ shí kuài qián.
turns.en: That's exactly what worries Xiaochuan. They've pushed the price down before anyone's even started. Right now a basket sells for over a hundred yuan. At their price, a weaver would make a few dozen yuan a day.

turns.name: 小雨
turns.hanzi: 还有一个问题：五千个，老人们根本编不完。到时候要么找外面的工厂，要么用机器，那还是竹溪的篮子吗？
turns.pinyin: hái yǒu yī gè wèntí: wǔ qiān gè, lǎorén men gēnběn biān bù wán. dàoshíhou yàome zhǎo wàimiàn de gōngchǎng, yàome yòng jīqì, nà háishi Zhúxī de lánzi ma?
turns.en: And there's another problem. The old weavers can't possibly make five thousand. Then it's either an outside factory or machines, and would they still be Zhuxi baskets?

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 我妈常说，篮子是有脾气的，每一个都不一样。要是变得跟工厂里出来的一模一样，人家为什么非买我们的不可呢？
turns.pinyin: wǒ mā cháng shuō, lánzi shì yǒu píqi de, měi yī gè dōu bù yīyàng. yàoshi biàn de gēn gōngchǎng lǐ chūlai de yīmúyīyàng, rénjiā wèishénme fēi mǎi wǒmen de bùkě ne?
turns.en: My mother always says that every basket has its own temper, and no two are the same. If they come out identical, like something from a factory, why would anyone insist on buying ours?

turns.name: 陈明
turns.hanzi: 可是反过来说，全球化就是这样：你想进入别人的市场，就得按别人的规矩来。我在伦敦开饭馆，菜单上不也得有甜酸肉吗？一点儿都不让步，生意就做不成。
turns.pinyin: kěshì fǎnguòláishuō, quánqiúhuà jiùshì zhèyàng: nǐ xiǎng jìnrù biéren de shìchǎng, jiù děi àn biéren de guīju lái. wǒ zài Lúndūn kāi fànguǎn, càidān shang bù yě děi yǒu tiánsuānròu ma? yīdiǎnr dōu bù ràngbù, shēngyi jiù zuò bù chéng.
turns.en: But look at it the other way round: that's globalisation. If you want to get into someone else's market, you play by their rules. When I opened a restaurant in London, didn't I have to put sweet and sour pork on the menu? If you won't give an inch, there's no deal.

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 让步可以，但是不能把自己让没了。甜酸肉你卖了，饺子可还是咱们家的饺子。越是民族的，越是世界的。
turns.pinyin: ràngbù kěyǐ, dànshì bù néng bǎ zìjǐ ràng méile. tiánsuānròu nǐ mài le, jiǎozi kě háishi zánmen jiā de jiǎozi. yuèshì mínzú de, yuèshì shìjiè de.
turns.en: Giving ground is fine, but not so much that there's nothing of you left. You sold the sweet and sour pork, but the dumplings were still our family's dumplings. The more something is your own, the more the world wants it.

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 我在伦敦的时候，看到很多东西都写着“中国制造”，又便宜又好用，可是没有人知道是谁做的。现在外国的顾客越来越想知道一个东西背后的故事。我觉得竹溪最值钱的，恰恰是这个故事。
turns.pinyin: wǒ zài Lúndūn de shíhou, kàn dào hěnduō dōngxi dōu xiě zhe zhōngguózhìzào, yòu piányi yòu hǎoyòng, kěshì méiyǒu rén zhīdào shì shéi zuò de. xiànzài wàiguó de gùkè yuèláiyuè xiǎng zhīdào yī gè dōngxi bèihòu de gùshi. wǒ juéde Zhúxī zuì zhíqián de, qiàqià shì zhège gùshi.
turns.en: When I was in London, I saw so many things marked 'Made in China', cheap and practical, but nobody knew who'd made them. Now customers abroad want more and more to know the story behind a thing. I think the most valuable thing Zhuxi has is precisely that story.

turns.name: 小雨
turns.hanzi: 那我们换个思路：与其贴牌，不如谈联名。篮子上同时出现两个品牌，每个篮子挂一张小卡片，写上编篮子的人的名字。
turns.pinyin: nà wǒmen huàn gè sīlù: yǔqí tiēpái, bùrú tán liánmíng. lánzi shang tóngshí chūxiàn liǎng gè pǐnpái, měi gè lánzi guà yī zhāng xiǎo kǎpiàn, xiě shàng biān lánzi de rén de míngzi.
turns.en: Then let's think about it differently. Rather than making for their brand, the co-op could talk about a co-brand. Both names on every basket, and a little card on each one with the name of the person who wove it.

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 那数量呢？
turns.pinyin: nà shùliàng ne?
turns.en: And the numbers?

turns.name: 陈明
turns.hanzi: 第一批先做一千个，全部手工编。价格可以谈，但是不能低于成本。他们要是真喜欢这个故事，就会接受。
turns.pinyin: dì yī pī xiān zuò yī qiān gè, quánbù shǒugōng biān. jiàgé kěyǐ tán, dànshì bù néng dīyú chéngběn. tāmen yàoshi zhēn xǐhuan zhège gùshi, jiù huì jiēshòu.
turns.en: A first batch of a thousand, all woven by hand. The price is negotiable, but not below cost. If they really like the story, they'll accept.

turns.name: 朵朵
turns.hanzi: 我可以把村里老人编篮子的视频剪一个英文版，发给他们看看。
turns.pinyin: wǒ kěyǐ bǎ cūn lǐ lǎorén biān lánzi de shìpín jiǎn yī gè yīngwénbǎn, fā gěi tāmen kàn kan.
turns.en: I can cut an English version of the video of the old people in the village weaving, and send it to them.

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 卡片上的英文交给我，我来写。
turns.pinyin: kǎpiàn shang de yīngwén jiāogěi wǒ, wǒ lái xiě.
turns.en: Leave the English on the cards to me. I'll write it.

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 好！我这就给小川回电话。成不成，就看他们识货不识货了。
turns.pinyin: hǎo! wǒ zhè jiù gěi Xiǎochuān huídiànhuà. chéng bù chéng, jiù kàn tāmen shíhuò bù shíhuò le.
turns.en: Good! I'll ring Xiaochuan back right now. Whether it comes off depends on whether they know a good thing when they see it.

turns.name: 朵朵
turns.hanzi: 马克，你看，还是那张桌子！四年前我就坐在那儿，躲在菜单后面看你。
turns.pinyin: Mǎkè, nǐ kàn, háishi nà zhāng zhuōzi! sì nián qián wǒ jiù zuò zài nà'ér, duǒ zài càidān hòumiàn kàn nǐ.
turns.en: Mark, look, it's the same table! Four years ago I was sitting right there, hiding behind a menu and watching you.

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 我记得。那天我在门口站了半天，不敢进来。
turns.pinyin: wǒ jìde. nà tiān wǒ zài ménkǒu zhàn le bàntiān, bù gǎn jìnlai.
turns.en: I remember. That day I stood at the door for ages, not daring to come in.

turns.name: 陈明
turns.hanzi: 马克，飞机上睡着了没有？我在对面饭馆里就看见你在这儿走来走去。
turns.pinyin: Mǎkè, fēijī shang shuìzháo le méiyǒu? wǒ zài duìmiàn fànguǎn lǐ jiù kànjiàn nǐ zài zhèr zǒuláizǒuqù.
turns.en: Mark, did you get any sleep on the plane? I could see you pacing up and down in here from the restaurant across the road.

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 睡不着。我在上海跟客户谈价格都不紧张，一想到要在这儿讲中文，手心就出汗。
turns.pinyin: shuìbuzháo. wǒ zài Shànghǎi gēn kèhù tán jiàgé dōu bù jǐnzhāng, yī xiǎng dào yào zài zhèr jiǎng zhōngwén, shǒuxīn jiù chūhàn.
turns.en: I couldn't sleep. In Shanghai I negotiate prices with clients without batting an eyelid, but when I think about speaking Chinese here, my palms start sweating.

turns.name: 陈爸爸
turns.hanzi: 放心吧，我们全家都坐第一排给你加油。马克第一次用中文演讲，我怎么能错过？你看，我连拐杖都没带。
turns.pinyin: fàngxīn ba, wǒmen quánjiā dōu zuò dìyīpái gěi nǐ jiāyóu. Mǎkè dì yī cì yòng zhōngwén yǎnjiǎng, wǒ zěnme néng cuòguò? nǐ kàn, wǒ lián guǎizhàng dōu méi dài.
turns.en: Relax. The whole family will be in the front row cheering you on. Mark's first speech in Chinese? How could I miss it? Look, I haven't even brought my stick.

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 稿子带了没有？别一上台，才想起来忘在饭馆里了。
turns.pinyin: gǎozi dài le méiyǒu? bié yī shàngtái, cái xiǎngqilai wàng zài fànguǎn lǐ le.
turns.en: Have you got your script? Don't get up on stage and then remember you've left it in the restaurant.

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 带了，带了，阿姨。其实演讲稿我早就背下来了。
turns.pinyin: dài le, dài le, āyí. qíshí yǎnjiǎnggǎo wǒ zǎojiù bèi xialai le.
turns.en: I've got it, Auntie, I've got it. Actually, I learned the speech by heart long ago.

turns.name: 小雨
turns.hanzi: 我还记得他刚来的时候，只会说“你好”和“谢谢”。
turns.pinyin: wǒ hái jìde tā gāng lái de shíhou, zhǐ huì shuō nǐhǎo hé xièxie.
turns.en: I still remember when he first came, all he could say was 'hello' and 'thank you'.

turns.name: 陈明
turns.hanzi: 还有“睡觉”。他点水饺的时候说的。
turns.pinyin: hái yǒu shuìjiào. tā diǎn shuǐjiǎo de shíhou shuō de.
turns.en: And 'sleep'. When he was ordering dumplings.

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 那件事你要说一辈子吗？
turns.pinyin: nà jiàn shì nǐ yào shuō yībèizi ma?
turns.en: Are you going to bring that up for the rest of my life?

turns.name: 朵朵
turns.hanzi: 马克，你今天要是说错了声调，我就在台下举手。
turns.pinyin: Mǎkè, nǐ jīntiān yàoshi shuōcuò le shēngdiào, wǒ jiù zài táixià jǔ shǒu.
turns.en: Mark, if you get a tone wrong today, I'm going to put my hand up in the audience.

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: ……朵朵，你还是坐最后一排吧。
turns.pinyin: Duǒduo, nǐ háishi zuò zuìhòu yī pái ba.
turns.en: ...Duoduo, I think you'd better sit in the back row.

turns.name: 陈妈妈
turns.hanzi: 小雨，你手上的项目上个月不是结束了吗？接下来有什么打算？
turns.pinyin: Xiǎoyǔ, nǐ shǒu shang de xiàngmù shàng gè yuè bùshì jiéshù le ma? jiēxiàlái yǒu shénme dǎsuàn?
turns.en: Xiaoyu, didn't your project finish last month? What are you planning next?

turns.name: 小雨
turns.hanzi: 这个嘛……中秋那天晚上，我在陈家饺子告诉大家。
turns.pinyin: zhège ma zhōngqiū nà tiān wǎnshang, wǒ zài Chénjiājiǎozi gàosu dàjiā.
turns.en: Well... I'll tell everyone on Mid-Autumn night, at Chen Family Dumplings.

turns.name: 陈明
turns.hanzi: 还卖关子！好，中秋晚上饭馆包场，谁都不许迟到。马克，特别是你。
turns.pinyin: hái màiguānzi! hǎo, zhōngqiū wǎnshang fànguǎn bāochǎng, shéi dōu bùxǔ chídào. Mǎkè, tèbiéshì nǐ.
turns.en: Keeping us in suspense! Right: on Mid-Autumn night the restaurant's closed for us, and nobody's allowed to be late. Mark, especially you.

turns.name: 朵朵
turns.hanzi: 马克，你看门口那个男生，在那儿站了十分钟了，一直不敢进来，跟你那时候一模一样。
turns.pinyin: Mǎkè, nǐ kàn ménkǒu nàge nánshēng, zài nàr zhàn le shí fēnzhōng le, yīzhí bù gǎn jìnlai, gēn nǐ nàshíhou yīmúyīyàng.
turns.en: Mark, look at the young man at the door. He's been standing there for ten minutes, too nervous to come in, just like you were.

turns.name: 马克
turns.hanzi: 我去吧。……你好！你也是来学中文的吧？别紧张，进来坐吧。
turns.pinyin: wǒ qù ba. nǐhǎo! nǐ yěshì lái xué zhōngwén de ba? bié jǐnzhāng, jìnlai zuò ba.
turns.en: I'll go... Hello! You're here to learn Chinese too, aren't you? Don't be nervous. Come in and sit down.

turns.name: 小雨
turns.hanzi: 四年前，走过去的人是我。
turns.pinyin: sì nián qián, zǒu guòqu de rén shì wǒ.
turns.en: Four years ago, I was the one who walked over.

readings.title: 这是我朋友
readings.py: zhè shì wǒ péng you
sentences: 吗|ma|turns a statement into a yes/no question

readings.translation: Chen Ming's dad: Hello, Courtyard Hotel. Mark: Hello! I'd like to book a room, checking in on the nineteenth of September, for five nights. Chen Ming's dad: Certainly: the nineteenth to the twenty-fourth, five nights. For how many people? Mark: Just me. Chen Ming's dad: Would you like a single room, a twin room, or a double? Mark: What's the difference between a twin and a double? Chen Ming's dad: A twin has two single beds, and a double has one big bed. The double is four hundred and eighty a night. It looks straight out onto the courtyard, and it's very quiet. Mark: Then I'll have the double. Does the rate include breakfast? Chen Ming's dad: It does. Breakfast is Beijing street food: soya milk, fried dough sticks, steamed buns. It's from seven to ten in the ground-floor dining room. Mark: Great! What time can I check in? My flight doesn't get in till nine in the evening. Chen Ming's dad: Any time after two. There's someone on reception twenty-four hours a day. Please bring your passport when you check in. There's also a five-hundred-yuan deposit, which we give back when you check out. Mark: Fine. My name's Mark Smith. What time is check-out? Chen Ming's dad: Before twelve noon. Mr Smith, you're all booked. We'll send you a confirmation text in a moment. ...Ha ha, you did really well! Now ring the hotel.

readings.translation: Dear Mr and Mrs Lin, Hello! I'm safely back in London. I've been getting over the jet lag these last few days, and today's the first chance I've had to write to you. First of all, thank you so much for your warm hospitality! In my nine days in Chengdu, Xiaoyu took me for hotpot, to see the pandas and round Kuanzhai Alley, and you invited me into your home for Mid-Autumn. I loved every dish Mrs Lin made, especially the twice-cooked pork. Mr Lin taught me to drink tea from a lidded bowl, and Chen Ming's dad even wore the same shirt as me! I'll always remember all of it. Before, I'd only read in books what a Chinese home is like. At your home, you made me feel I wasn't a guest, but one of the family. That Mid-Autumn evening, when we ate mooncakes and looked at the moon together, was the most memorable night of my trip. After I left Chengdu I spent five days in Beijing. On the last evening, Chen Ming's mum and dad took me for roast duck. Chen Ming was right: Beijing roast duck is delicious! But the food I miss most is still Mrs Lin's cooking. Xiaoyu's back in London the day after tomorrow. You're welcome to come and visit London one day, and when you do, I'll treat you to Chen Ming's dumplings! The photos are attached. Have a look. Thank you again! Wishing you good health and all the best! Mark 26 September

readings.translation: These last few days, lots of friends have asked me: what's the difference between a qipao, hanfu and a Tang jacket? Today I'll explain, simply. Hanfu is the oldest, with two or three thousand years of history, much older than the qipao. Hanfu is usually long, with wide, full sleeves. It looks wonderful on, but it isn't as practical as a qipao. In the last few years more and more young people have started wearing hanfu to take photos in the park, and some even wear it out and about. The qipao became fashionable in Shanghai a hundred years ago. It's much shorter than hanfu, and much tighter, with a fairly high collar. Many women used to wear a qipao every day. Now it's mostly for weddings or special events. Both men and women can wear a Tang jacket. It has the character 唐 in its name, but it has very little to do with the Tang dynasty. Chinese people living abroad used to call themselves 'Tang people', which is where we get 'Tang people street', Chinatown, and also the 'Tang jacket'. What am I wearing to my graduation show opening? My mum's sent me a red qipao from Chengdu, so that's the one! My cousin's wearing his Tang jacket. And Mark? He says it's a secret.

readings.translation: Chen Ming's dad: Duoduo and I spent the whole morning looking at oil paintings in the National Gallery. My eyes are tired. What about you? Mark: We've been looking at Chinese paintings. Xiaoyu, what exactly is the difference between Chinese painting and oil painting? Xiǎo Yǔ: First, the tools are different. Chinese painting uses a brush and ink, usually on paper. Oil painting uses oil paints, on canvas. Duoduo: And the colours! Oil paintings have lots of strong colour, and a lot of Chinese paintings only use black. Xiǎo Yǔ: But there's more than one kind of black in Chinese painting. Ink can be dark or pale, and painters use dark and pale to show what's near and far. Mark: And the empty space. Oil painters usually cover the whole canvas, and Chinese painting likes to leave some parts unpainted. Chen Ming's dad: Right. Lots of oil painters want to paint exactly what they see. Xiǎo Yǔ: Chinese painters are a bit different. Qi Baishi said the best painting is somewhere between 'like' and 'not like'. Chen Ming's dad: Interesting! What about Xu Beihong, then? What he studied in Paris was oil painting. Xiǎo Yǔ: Yes. He brought Western ways of painting into Chinese painting, so his horses are both true to life and full of energy. Mark: East meets West! Just like Xiaoyu's graduation show: London painted the Chinese way. Duoduo: So which of you two can do Chinese painting? Xiǎo Yǔ: I can a bit. Mark, Duoduo, next time I'll teach you to paint shrimps! Mark: Great! But my shrimps will definitely be somewhere between 'like' and 'not like'... more like fish!

readings.translation: Mark: Happy New Year! Wishing you both a very happy New Year! Chen Ming's dad: Thank you, thank you, Happy New Year! Here, this red envelope is for you. Mark: No, no, I can't! I'm a grown man. How can I take a red envelope from you? Chen Ming's mum: If you're not married, you're still a child! Go on, take it. It's New Year money, for luck. Duoduo: Mark, you can't refuse a red envelope from your elders. Watch me: take it with both hands and say 'thank you, Grandpa'. That's all. Mark: Well... thank you! Wishing you both good health, and may everything go well for you! Chen Ming's mum: Oh, what a sweet talker! Come and have breakfast. There are still loads of dumplings. Mark: More dumplings? I ate over thirty last night and didn't get a single coin... Chen Ming's dad: Then keep eating today! Oh, by the way, could you follow the gala last night? Mark: Everything except the comic dialogues. They talk too fast. Chen Ming: Comic dialogues are full of Beijing slang. It's normal not to understand them. Mark: And at midnight I only heard a few firecrackers. I thought there'd be firecrackers going off everywhere in Beijing at New Year. Chen Ming's dad: It used to be like that. The hutongs were full of firecrackers. Now you can't set them off in town, for safety and for the air. If you want to, you have to go a long way out. Chen Ming's mum: It's better without them, safer and cleaner. Come on, come on, eat up. Dumplings are no good once they've gone cold!

readings.translation: Xiǎo Yǔ: Mark, Happy New Year! Look, I'm playing the guitar for my mum and dad. Mark: Happy New Year! Hello to your mum and dad! Xiaoyu, I heard the erhu today. How many strings has your guitar got? Xiǎo Yǔ: Six. The erhu's only got two, but it can make so many different sounds. It's much harder than the guitar. Mark: You play the erhu with a bow? I thought you plucked it. Xiǎo Yǔ: The erhu's bowed, and the guzheng and the guitar are plucked. I learned the guzheng for two years when I was little. It's still in my room. Mark: Really? Then play me something! Xiǎo Yǔ: I haven't played for ages... I'll give it a go. ...How was that? Mark: It sounds beautiful, like gentle rain falling! Xiǎo Yǔ: Ha ha, thanks! Oh, did you see the face-changing? Mark: I did! I still can't work out how it's done. You're from Sichuan. Do you know? Xiǎo Yǔ: I've seen it loads of times and I can't tell either. They say the way it's done is a secret, and they don't usually teach it to outsiders. Mark: I can't understand a word of Beijing opera, but the erhu and the guzheng, I understand them fine. Xiǎo Yǔ: Exactly. Good music doesn't need translating. Everyone understands it! Mark: Well said! Then play another one. I'll listen here in Beijing, and it'll be like we're spending New Year together!

The drawings are really good. Mark: Right, I'll take it. Is there an English version too? I want to read the Chinese and English side by side. Duoduo: The foreign-language books are over there. readings.translation: Saturday 29 January. Sunny, minus eight. Today I finally climbed the Great Wall! When I came to Beijing last September I didn't have time, and I've been sorry ever since. This time Chen Ming, his dad and Duoduo took me to Mutianyu. Mutianyu isn't as crowded as Badaling, and in winter there are even fewer visitors. The Wall was even steeper than I'd imagined. At first I didn't think it was hard at all, but the higher we climbed, the steeper the steps and the stronger the wind. After an hour, I was so tired I couldn't feel my legs, but nine-year-old Duoduo was out in front the whole way. Beside me, Chen Ming said: 'Keep going! You're not a hero till you've climbed the Great Wall!' '不到长城非好汉' is a very famous line from a poem. 非 means 'is not', and a 好汉 is someone brave and remarkable. It means: anyone who hasn't been to the Great Wall isn't a hero. These days, lots of people use it to say: don't be afraid of hard things, and keep going to the end. At the highest watchtower, I looked down: the Wall was like a dragon, running from one mountain all the way to the next. At that moment I felt that however tired I was, it had been worth it. On the way down I took the cable car with Chen Ming's dad, which was quick and comfortable. Now I'm a hero too! Though tomorrow I might not be able to walk...

readings.translation: Chen Ming's dad: What a lot of people reporting crimes. Let's look at this form first. I often help people fill it in at the community centre. I'll ask, you answer, as if I were the officer. You're here to report a crime, I take it? What was stolen? Mark: My phone. At about half past six yesterday evening, on the Northern line. Chen Ming's dad: What kind of phone? Mark: A black one. I've had it just over a year. It's got a blue case on it, and there's a bank card in the case too. Chen Ming's dad: Have you reported the card lost? Mark: I did it last night, and I locked the phone online too. Chen Ming's dad: Good. Next question: did you notice anyone odd near you at the time? Mark: No. The carriage was really crowded and I was reading the whole time. I didn't notice a thing. Chen Ming's dad: Reading, on a train that packed? Honestly, you! Mark: Uncle, does this happen a lot? Chen Ming's dad: Quite a lot. My wallet got nicked the year before last too, and it's never turned up. Thieves usually strike when people are getting on and off. The more crowded it is, the easier it is to get robbed. Mark: So is there any chance of getting my phone back? Chen Ming's dad: To be honest, not much. Fill in this form first, and if the police hear anything they'll let you know straight away. ...Hey, you can say all this in Chinese now. Not bad! Mark: I've been learning for nearly two years. Next month I'm presenting our designs to a client in Shanghai, in Chinese. Chen Ming's dad: Then good luck with it! You can always buy another phone, but the Chinese you've learned, nobody can steal that.

readings.translation: I've been learning Chinese for nearly two years. Three months ago, for the first time, I presented our design proposal to a client in Shanghai in Chinese. Lately friends keep asking me: 'What's your secret?' Actually, there's nothing magic about my secrets, and there are only four of them. First, learn a little every day. I'm busy at work, so I just listen to a podcast for twenty minutes on the Tube every day and learn ten new words. Twenty minutes isn't long, but over a year, it adds up to more than a hundred hours. Second, don't be afraid of getting it wrong. At first I made mistakes all the time. I even once said 'sleep' instead of 'dumplings'. My friends laughed, helped me put it right, and I've never forgotten it since. Third, find a good teacher and good friends. I met Xiaoyu at the language exchange. She's taught me for two years and has never once laughed at my pronunciation. I've eaten Mrs Lin's twice-cooked pork in Chengdu, and spent Spring Festival with Chen Ming's family in Beijing. Experiences like these have made me more and more interested in Chinese. Fourth, learn about what you love. I love food, so the first things I learned were the names of dishes. If you love music, listen to Chinese songs. If you love films, watch Chinese films. Now I'm learning how to write work emails in Chinese. Learning Chinese is like climbing the Great Wall: the higher you go, the more tiring it gets, but the view gets better and better too. Keep going!

readings.translation: Chen Ming's dad: Look, you can see the sea from the garden! Xiaoyu, this house you found for us is really nice. Xiǎo Yǔ: It's close to my place too, just ten minutes' walk. My flatmate's gone back to China for New Year, so Mark can have her room. Mark: Xiaoyu's always saying Chen Ming's dumplings are the best in the whole of London. They taste just as good in Melbourne! Chen Ming: Of course! I'm not bragging, but there are no more authentic dumplings in London than mine. Mark: Chen Ming, Xiaoyu and I have been discussing all day whether Melbourne or London is better. What do you think? Chen Ming: Need you ask? London, of course! Take food: London has every kind of food there is, for instance... Xiǎo Yǔ: Melbourne's just the same! People here come from all over the world. Italian, Greek, Vietnamese: whatever you fancy, it's here. Chen Ming: What about Chinese food? London's Chinatown is really lively, and it's got Chen Family Dumplings! Xiǎo Yǔ: Melbourne's Chinatown has a longer history! It's been here since the 1850s, built by the Chinese who came in the gold rush. Chen Ming: Really? I honestly didn't know that. What about the weather, then? Melbourne must be unbearably hot in summer? Mark: That's true, sometimes it's pretty hot. But it's much nicer than winter in Beijing. Last Spring Festival I was so cold on the Great Wall I couldn't speak! Chen Ming's dad: What's wrong with cold? If you ask me, Beijing's better than anywhere. It's got the Great Wall and Beijing opera. London and Melbourne can't compare! Chen Ming's mum: All right, all right, eat your dumplings. I reckon it doesn't matter which city is best. What matters is who you're with. Mark: I couldn't agree more! Wherever you lot are, that's the best city. Chen Ming: Ha ha, Mark, your Chinese is getting smoother by the day!

readings.translation: Mark: Xiaoyu, Duoduo's Chinese class sounds really good fun. I heard those kids talking. Their Chinese is more natural than mine! Xiǎo Yǔ: Most of them speak Chinese at home. It was different for their teacher, Ms Huang, when she was little. Her family spoke Cantonese, and she only learned Mandarin after she went to university. Mark: Really? No wonder her English name is Lily Wong, not Huang. Xiǎo Yǔ: Yes, in Cantonese 黄 is pronounced Wong. Her family's been in Australia for over a hundred years. They say the first one to come here came for the gold. Mark: So that's how it is! Oh, by the way, your colleagues all call you 小林, but everyone at the restaurant calls Chen Ming 老陈. He's only thirty-something. So is he old or not? Xiǎo Yǔ: Ha ha, neither 老 nor 小 is about age here. They call him 老陈 because they're close. But to his mum he'll always be a child. She still calls him 小明 even now. Mark: 老 is a busy little word! Teacher, boss, tiger, mouse... and mice aren't old at all. Xiǎo Yǔ: That 老 doesn't really mean anything. It's just a prefix. There are suffixes too, like 家: painter, writer, scientist. Mark: 者 as well, right? Author, reader, journalist, and me two years ago: a beginner! Xiǎo Yǔ: You stopped being a beginner long ago. Here are two more: 化 and 性. 现代 plus 化 makes... Mark: 现代化, modernisation! So 国际化 means becoming more international? Xiǎo Yǔ: Exactly! Melbourne's a very international city. And 性: take 重要性 and 可能性. They're about how important something is, how likely it is. Mark: I get it! Once you've learned these, you can work out what new words mean. Xiǎo Yǔ: Exactly. Why don't you come along next week? Duoduo's already told the other kids she's got a 'laowai pupil'!

readings.translation: Chen Ming's dad: Come in, come in! Hot out there, isn't it? It's only three degrees in London right now and thirty-five here. I still haven't got used to it. Mark: Happy New Year! This is for you and your wife, just a little something. Wishing you good health! Chen Ming's dad: Oh, you shouldn't have! Coming is enough. Why bring anything? Chen Ming: Mark, Xiaoyu, sit down. Duoduo, come here and wish them a happy new year! Duoduo: Mark, Xiaoyu, Happy New Year! Wishing you... lots of money! Xiǎo Yǔ: What a good girl! Here, this red envelope is from me. Mark: And this one's from me. Duoduo, I hope school goes well this year! Duoduo: Thank you! Granny, can I open them? Chen Ming's mum: You mustn't open them in front of the guests. It's rude. Give them to Granny, and Granny will look after them for you. Chen Ming: Ha ha, it's the same every year. As soon as she gets a red envelope, Granny 'looks after' it. Mark: Chen Ming, I've been meaning to ask: in China, how much do people usually put in a red envelope? Chen Ming: It depends on the relationship. For children, one or two hundred is enough. It's best to use an even number, like two hundred or six hundred. Eight is the most popular, because 八 sounds like the 发 in 发财, to get rich. Mark: What about four hundred, then? ...Only joking. I know four's unlucky. Chen Ming's mum: Ha ha, for a laowai you know a lot! Come on, have some dumplings. I've made three hundred today!

readings.translation: 一格设计 was founded in 2016 and is based by Suzhou Creek in Shanghai. We are a specialist brand design agency, providing brand strategy, visual design, packaging design and other services to clients in China and abroad. Our clients range from brands with decades of history to new brands just starting out. We are a young, international team of more than twenty people from cities in China and abroad. Here, every good idea has a chance to become real work. As our business grows, we are now recruiting a junior designer, based in Shanghai. Duties: 1. Visual design for brand projects, including posters, packaging and social media images. 2. Working with senior designers to complete design proposals, and taking part in discussing and revising them. 3. Keeping in good contact with clients and completing work on time. Requirements: 1. A degree or above in design or a related subject; this year's graduates welcome. 2. Skilled in common design software. 3. A good eye, good communication skills and a sense of responsibility, and able to handle a fairly fast pace of work. 4. Internship experience in brand design or at an advertising agency preferred. 5. Ability to read work materials in English preferred. We offer: a competitive salary, full social insurance and housing fund, paid annual leave, flexible hours, and the chance to work with an international team. Every new employee has one-to-one mentoring from an experienced designer. If you're interested, please send your CV and portfolio to our recruitment email address by 31 March, with 'Junior designer application + your name' in the subject line. We will contact suitable candidates within a week of receiving applications.

readings.translation: At nine in the evening, office blocks in many big cities are still ablaze with light. For quite a few young people, overtime has become part of life. Some even joke that if they aren't working late, they're on their way to work late. You can't talk about overtime without mentioning 996. This way of working was once very common at some tech companies, and it has always been highly controversial. Supporters argue that putting up with some hardship while you're young not only teaches you more, but also gets you promoted and paid more, faster. Especially in fiercely competitive industries, whether a project is finished on time can affect the growth of the whole company. Opponents argue that long hours damage people's health, and also leave them no time for their families or their own interests. Besides, when people are tired, their efficiency is bound to drop. Working long hours doesn't mean achieving more. Legally, China's labour law sets clear rules on working hours, overtime is limited, and companies should pay overtime or give time off in lieu. In recent years 996 has come in for more and more criticism, and the authorities have stressed many times that overtime must comply with the law. So how should we really see overtime? Perhaps the answer isn't a simple yes or no. Most people can understand working late for a few days now and then for an important project. But if overtime becomes the norm, or even a performance put on for the boss, it's worth stopping to think: what are we working so hard for? Does your company often work late? What do you think of 996? Tell us in the comments.

readings.translation: Dear Manager Wang, Good afternoon. Thank you for your valuable comments on our design proposal of 11 May. This morning the designer Lin Xiaoyu and I held a meeting especially to discuss them, and our managing director has approved the changes we propose. The results are as follows. 1. Main colour: we will adjust the colour as you requested and, based on the results of last month's market survey, provide two different versions for you to choose from. 2. Brand name: in the new design, the brand name will be enlarged to make the packaging more eye-catching. 3. Delivery: regarding your request to bring the gift box deadline forward by a week, we are confirming production times with the printers. As the colour change may affect printing costs, we will let you know the details separately by Tuesday 15 May. 4. English description: following your previous comments, we have added a short English description to the gift box, to make it easier for foreigners working in Shanghai to give as a present. The revised design will be sent to you by Wednesday 16 May. The minutes of today's meeting are attached. To make sure the project is completed on time, we suggest a video call between our two teams on the afternoon of Friday 18 May to confirm the revised design. The exact time can be set to suit your schedule. If convenient, the printers' manager could join us too. If you have any questions, please contact me at any time. Thank you once again for your trust and support. We look forward to continuing to work with you. With best regards, (respectful greetings) Mark, 一格设计 14 May 2029

readings.translation: This week I made an important decision: the third restaurant can wait. Here's what happened. Two weeks ago a company contacted me, wanting to go into partnership and open another Chen Family Dumplings in Hangzhou. My income might be half as much again as it is now. I'd be lying if I said I wasn't tempted. In Shanghai, the rent, the staff's wages, each day's vegetables: what doesn't cost money? Several friends of mine with restaurants have opened a second and a third, and they're always urging me to earn as much as I can while I'm young. But when I calmed down and thought about it, that kind of life doesn't fit my idea of running a restaurant at all. What I love most is standing in the kitchen, making a flavour that belongs to our family, not sitting in an office all day in meetings, looking at the numbers on a phone app and discussing which button should go where. Rather than opening three restaurants I've no time to go to, I'd do better to make the two I have even better. Of course, passion alone isn't enough: the rent still has to be paid. So I plucked up my courage and had a talk with the company. To my surprise, they weren't annoyed at all. They've even agreed to help promote the Shanghai restaurant first, and Hangzhou can wait. I can put my whole heart into getting Shanghai right, and I've gained a partner too: two birds with one stone. Some people say you mustn't be half-hearted, and that a restaurant needs a full three years before you open the next. I don't entirely agree. There's nothing wrong with opening a new restaurant in itself. What matters is being clear about what you want, and that's true in any field. If you just want to start again somewhere else because you're tired or fed up, you may well be giving up halfway. But if you know where you're going, go boldly. As for me? I'd rather go a bit more slowly and walk the road I've chosen. Finally, thank you to my daughter, who asked a question I had never thought about. And thanks to our family's British friend, who leaves work on the dot of six every day. He once said something I really like: 'We work in order to live, not live in order to work.'

readings.translation: On 1 July 2019, Shanghai's regulations on household waste came into force, and Shanghai became one of the first cities in China to make rubbish sorting compulsory. Ten years on, sorting has gone from a novelty to part of everyday life for Shanghai people. Under the regulations, household waste is divided into four kinds: recyclables, hazardous waste, wet rubbish and dry rubbish. Residents must sort and put out their rubbish according to the rules, or they may be fined. Because each kind of rubbish is dealt with differently, sorting has to start in every home. At first, many people found it hard to adjust. 'What kind of rubbish are you?' was for a time the most popular phrase online, and some people even downloaded special apps so they could look up every item before they threw it away. Many estates brought in collection at set times and places, and every day volunteers in red waistcoats stood by the bin stores, checking and patiently explaining. Ten years on, the change is plain to see. Wet rubbish goes to special plants and becomes fertiliser and energy; recyclables are processed and return to people's lives. The amount of rubbish sent to landfill has fallen sharply, and the streets are cleaner. More importantly, sorting has made many people stop and think: how much do we actually throw away every day? Of course, problems remain. There are more and more takeaways and deliveries, and disposable food boxes, plastic bags and cardboard boxes pile up every day. Because much packaging is hard to recycle, experts believe sorting is only the first step, and the key is to cut waste at the source. So what can ordinary people do? Take your own cup and shopping bag when you go out, so you use fewer disposable things; choose 'no cutlery' when you order a takeaway; and before you buy something, ask yourself whether you really need it. These are small things, but they're worth everyone doing. As someone once put it, sorting rubbish doesn't just sort rubbish: it sorts our habits too.

readings.translation: My home village, Zhuxi, lies deep in the hills of western Zhejiang. It is surrounded by bamboo, and when the wind blows, the leaves rustle all over the mountainside. When I was a child, every family farmed, and every family wove baskets. Every morning my mother went up the hill to cut bamboo, and every afternoon she sat at the door weaving. My sister and I sat beside her on little stools doing our homework, and watched the strips of bamboo slowly turn into a basket in her hands. Later my sister got into secondary school in the county town, then went to university in Chengdu. The year I turned nineteen I went to Beijing to find work, and I have been away for more than forty years. Each time I came home, the village was quieter than the time before: the young people had gone, houses stood empty, and the village primary school had closed. My mother says only a dozen or so people in the whole village can still weave baskets, and the youngest is over sixty. After my generation left, the next one left too, and left its children with their grandparents. The days before Spring Festival are the happiest of those children's year: their parents come home after a whole day on the coach, with new clothes and snacks from the city. But once the fifteenth of the first month has passed, they have to leave again. The grown-ups call children like these 'left-behind children'. As urbanisation has gone on, more and more people have left the countryside to look for opportunities in the cities. It has given many families a better life, and that's how I got out too. But while the cities are growing up, the villages are growing old. That is nobody's fault: it is the choice of an era. In the last few years, things have started to change. My brother's son came back from Hangzhou, and every evening he sells bamboo baskets on a livestream. The co-operative has brought the old weavers together, buying and selling their work as one. My mother is eighty-five this year. The first time she saw someone buy one of her baskets on a phone, she couldn't stop smiling. We hope this brand can do one small thing: when someone in the city picks up a bamboo basket, they'll also think of the hands in the hills that wove it.

readings.translation: Before I came to Shanghai, all I knew of the city was the Bund and Lujiazui in photographs: skyscrapers, lights, boats on the Huangpu. Seven months after arriving, I have discovered that the real Shanghai isn't on the postcards, but in its lanes, one after another. My lane is just off Yuyuan Road. A little after six every morning, it wakes up: bicycle bells, the sound of cooking, aunties greeting each other in Shanghainese, all pouring in through the window at once. When I first moved in, I couldn't understand a word. The talk just sounded soft, as if people were singing. Now I can understand 'nong ho', 'alah' and 'shia shia nong'. My landlady is a good friend's mother, and I call her Auntie. She moved here only a few months ago, and she is already the lane's housekeeper: whose rubbish hasn't been sorted properly, whose grandson has got into university, she knows it all. The first time I put my rubbish in the wrong bin, she was the one who stopped me; when I caught a cold later, she was the one who brought me a bowl of steaming chicken soup. With her, I'm part tenant, part son. Autumn is when I love Shanghai most. The plane trees along the roads stand tall, their leaves slowly turn yellow, and when the wind blows they come down one by one. Walking beneath them, I can't help thinking of the streets of London, which are lined with the very same trees. In Shanghai people call it the French plane; in London its name is the London plane. One tree, two names: it's as if it joins my two cities together. Of course, Shanghai has its headaches too: the summers are hot and muggy, the morning metro is so packed you can't move, and the rent is painfully expensive. But whenever I cycle to work along Suzhou Creek and watch the sunlight brighten bit by bit on the water, I feel again that it's all worth it. Seven months ago, Shanghai was just an unfamiliar name to me. Today it is my lane, my neighbours, my breakfast, my plane trees. I don't know how much longer I'll live here, but I know that wherever I go in the future, I'll say: this is my Shanghai.

readings.translation: Last Saturday morning I took the old man of our house to hospital about his knees, and the outpatients' hall was packed with patients. An old man in his eighties stood in front of a self-service machine for a long time, holding an old envelope. Inside was a neat stack of cash, and a note his daughter had written him: 'Dad, scan the code to register first.' But his phone was a ten-year-old phone for the elderly, and couldn't scan anything. I took him to the staffed counter. As he counted out his money, he kept saying sorry: he was causing everyone trouble, everything needed a phone now, and old people couldn't keep up. Hearing that, I felt awful. Over the last ten years or so, mobile payment has changed life in China. Breakfast, the metro, the bills: you just take out your phone and scan. In Shanghai many young people haven't touched cash for years, and since I came here I've been the same. For most people it has been a huge convenience. But while we enjoy the convenience, some people have been left behind. China has more than three hundred million people over sixty, and many of them can't, or daren't, use a smartphone. For them, one little QR code can be an invisible barrier. In fact, it isn't that older people can't learn. I've found that as long as someone teaches them patiently, many learn fast. The old man of our house is nearly seventy and always refused to pay by phone, and he has just learned to scan a code from eleven-year-old Duoduo. He says it's 'a nuisance', but the next day he went and bought breakfast with it all by himself. What older people need isn't necessarily more advanced technology. It's a bit more time and a bit more patience. Luckily, a lot of places have started to change. The rules say shops may not refuse cash, and this hospital has kept its staffed counters, with volunteers by the machines to help. Technology should serve people. It shouldn't make anyone feel that, because they can't keep up with it, they've become a nuisance. That day, as he left, the old man carefully put the envelope back in his pocket, called me 'young lady', thanked me again and again, and said that when he got home he'd ask his grandson to teach him. I hope that next time he comes, whether he pays in cash or by phone, he won't have to say sorry.

readings.translation: From 12 December to 10 January I went a whole thirty days without scrolling short videos. It started with a bet over dinner with a British friend. Now I can proudly announce: I won. The first week was the hardest. Every night I lay down, my finger used to open that app all by itself. After I deleted it, I'd still pick up my phone, unlock it, stare at it blankly and put it down again. That's when I realised I really was a bit hooked. From the second week, things slowly started to change. I was asleep before midnight every night, and I stopped waking up with headaches. In the forty minutes on the way to and from work, I finished two books. I used to say I had no time to read, but the time was there all along. It had just been chopped into fifteen-second pieces. Of course, giving up short video has its price. When my friends talked about the latest viral video in our group chat, I couldn't join in at all; and some videos, teaching cooking or exercise, were actually quite useful. Besides, short video isn't a bad thing in itself. A relative of ours, back in the family's village in Zhejiang, has used it to sell baskets woven by old people in the hills all over the country. So I think the problem doesn't lie in short video, but in whether we can still control ourselves. The algorithm knows what we want to watch, but it doesn't care what we need. However good an app is, it shouldn't be the one deciding where our time goes. Now I've downloaded the app again, but I've set myself two rules: half an hour a day at most, and nothing after eleven at night. Rather than fighting my phone, I'd rather make a deal with it. Oh, and two other people were in the bet with me. Eleven-year-old Duoduo went a whole month without playing games, so she won too; her grandma lasted just five days, and said there was one health video she 'simply had to watch'. The British friend has already bought the whole family milk tea. He says next month we're having another bet: who can go a month without ordering takeaway.

readings.translation: Colleagues, good afternoon! Today I'd like to discuss one question with you: will artificial intelligence replace designers? To be honest, I've asked myself that many times this past year. First, a fact: AI has already changed the way we work. Sketches that used to take a team a week can now be generated by the dozen in minutes. For clients, that means faster and cheaper; for design agencies, it means pressure like never before. Some say designers will disappear, like typists before them. I don't agree. Every advance in technology does away with some jobs, and at the same time creates new ones. That said, we can't pretend nothing has happened. The first to feel it are often young people just starting out, because what AI does best is precisely that repetitive groundwork. So what can't AI do? As I see it, at least three things. First, it doesn't ask questions. Good design often starts with a good question: who is this brand, really? Who does it want to talk to? Second, it can't judge. It can give you a hundred answers, but it doesn't know which one is right. Third, it can't take responsibility. When a design goes wrong, the client comes looking for a person, not a machine. So rather than worrying about being replaced, let's be clear about what only people can do. And the other way round: the things AI does faster and better, let's hand over to it without a second thought. But we have a duty to young designers too: we mustn't stop giving them the chance to practise just because AI can draw sketches. Of course, many questions have no answer yet. Whose work did AI learn to draw from? What should those artists get? These questions need answers from the law, and careful thought from every one of us. When all's said and done, AI is a tool, like the pen in our hand. Tools will keep getting more powerful, but deciding what to draw, who to draw it for and why should always be up to people. Thank you!

readings.translation: Our reporter writes: With the New Year approaching, Zhuxi village in the hills of western Zhejiang is far busier than in previous years. According to the village's bamboo-weaving co-operative, in the month to 20 January it sold more than 8,000 bamboo baskets, fruit trays and other items by online livestream, with sales of over 600,000 yuan, five times the figure for the same period last year. Zhuxi is surrounded by bamboo forest, and villagers have woven baskets for several hundred years. As young people left to work elsewhere, only a dozen or so elderly weavers remained, and the craft was at one point in danger of dying out. The turning point came last year. In summer 2029 the village set up a bamboo-weaving co-operative to buy and sell the weavers' work together, and asked a Shanghai design agency to create a new brand and packaging for its products. In early December, villager Wu Chuan posted a short video online of his grandmother weaving a basket, and it quickly passed three million views. It is understood that Wu returned home from Hangzhou three years ago and sells bamboo ware by livestream every evening. Wu said that a stream used to get a few dozen viewers and now often has two or three thousand, and that on the busiest day he received more than a thousand orders. The surge in orders has brought new problems. The head of the co-operative said that the old weavers can make two or three a day at most, so many orders won't ship until after Spring Festival; the co-operative was organising young people in the village to learn to weave, and more than twenty had already signed up. Experts believe short video has brought new opportunities for rural crafts, but that traffic comes and goes quickly; whether an internet hit can become a lasting brand, they say, still depends on quality. It is understood that the co-operative plans to open bamboo-weaving classes for visitors this spring, and welcomes people from the cities to come and learn.

readings.translation: Son: it's late, and I expect you're still at the restaurant. Some things I can't bring myself to say to your face, and the moment I open my mouth we'd only end up arguing, so I want to write them down. Read this slowly when you have time. Over those three days at Qingming I 'picked out' someone for Xiaoyu, and then started on you over dinner. Thinking about it now, Mum was in too much of a hurry. Anyone would have had enough. These last few days you've come home late and said very little, and it hurts. You may think we're old-fashioned. But you should know how your dad and I got married. In 1993 I was an accountant at a factory in Beijing, and an older colleague introduced me to your dad. We met three times, went to one film, and six months later we were married. In those days that's how everyone did it. Nobody asked whether you were in love, only whether you were suited. In all these years we've had plenty of rows, and been through plenty of hard times together, but looking back, having someone beside you gives you peace of mind. That's why we've always hoped you'd have someone beside you too. Every time a relative asks about you and says, 'Chen Ming has so much going for him, how come he's still on his own?', I smile, and then at night I can't sleep. Xiaoyu said the other day that she hates the phrase 'leftover woman'. The truth is, so do I. She has made her own way in Shanghai and stood on her own two feet. How could she be 'left over'? It's the same with you: you've brought Duoduo up on your own, and nobody can say you aren't doing well. When it comes down to it, what Mum fears isn't that you won't marry. It's that you'll have too hard a time on your own: nobody to bring you a glass of water when you're ill, nobody to talk to when you're sad. When your dad and I are old, and gone, and Duoduo has grown up, who'll keep you company? But these last few days I've come to see something clearly: marriage isn't a task, and you can't just pick anyone for the sake of getting it done. Times have changed, after all. Your generation has its own ideas and its own choices. Rather than push you both into meeting people you don't like, better to let you live the lives you want. I know I nag. From now on, I won't arrange any more dates for either of you, and I'll have a proper word with your aunt about Xiaoyu too. If the relatives ask again, I'll say: my son is doing very well. If you meet someone you like, bring them home for us to see; if you don't, that's all right too. There'll always be a hot meal waiting for you at home. However old you are, your dad and I keep you in our thoughts. Come home and get an early night, and don't stay so late at the restaurant all the time. Mum

readings.translation: On the morning of 7 June 2021, I stood at the door of the exam hall in a secondary school in Chengdu, holding a clear plastic folder with my admission ticket and two black pens inside. Mum had got up before dawn to boil me two eggs to go with a fried dough stick: 'a hundred per cent', she called it, one and two zeros. That year, more than ten million candidates across the country walked into exam halls, just like me. For me, the gaokao was a race I had been running for twelve years. But for my desk-mate, the gaokao was a bridge. Her home was a county town deep in the mountains. At this end of the bridge were her grandmother's courtyard, and parents she saw once a year; at the other end was university, a world she had only seen on television. She'd never been to a cram class as a child, her family couldn't afford a tutor, and all she had to go on was her own score. Some say the gaokao is unfair, but for children like her it's precisely the fairest road there is: it doesn't ask whose child you are, it only looks at your paper. Of course, it was no easy road. In our final year we got up at half past five and lights went out at half past ten. On the board at the back of the classroom was the countdown, and every day less meant a little more pressure. Some classmates lay awake all night with the stress, and one girl fell ill a month before the exam. Since coming to Shanghai, I've found that children today have it even harder. My cousin's daughter is only eleven, and she has four cram classes at the weekend. Parents say it isn't that they want to push their children; they have no choice: everyone else is running, and if you stop, your child gets left behind. But when everyone pushes forward as hard as they can, nobody gets a single step ahead. That's what's called 'involution'. Although the government has brought in the 'double reduction' policy to cut homework and outside tutoring, as long as the competition for school places remains, it's hard for parents' anxiety to really go away. I often think that the gaokao bridge let children like my desk-mate walk out of the mountains, and that is the most precious thing about it. But a bridge shouldn't become the only road in life. Your score can decide which university you go to, but it can't decide what kind of person you'll become. In a month's time, another ten million and more young people will walk into the exam halls. I'd like to say to them: just do your best. On the other side of the bridge, the road is long, and wide.

readings.translation: My dad had his operation last week. For ten days I've been keeping him company on the orthopaedic ward, and I've seen every kind of filial duty. Some children phone ten times a day but never once come in; some take long leave and sleep on a folding chair by the bed for a month. And there's one woman in her sixties whose mother, in her eighties, is in hospital: every day she spends an hour and a half on the bus to bring her food, and often forgets to take her own blood-pressure pills. This is what many Chinese families look like today. As the one-child generation reaches middle age, a couple often has four elderly parents above them and a child below. With the old above and the young below, those in the middle are the most exhausted. I'm the same: my parents above, my daughter below, and a restaurant in between. Traditionally, Chinese people have believed in 'raising children to provide for old age': being filial meant staying by your parents and caring for them with your own hands. But now many children work in other cities, even abroad, and couldn't stay close if they wanted to. And so there are more and more 'empty-nest elderly': the children have gone, the home is empty, and only an old couple are left, or just one. That was how my parents lived in Beijing during my first few years in London. So is sending your parents to a care home a failure of duty? Many people can't get over that hurdle in their hearts, and my dad is one of them. But on the ward I often think: a care home isn't so much a place for people 'nobody wants' as another kind of care. Professional nursing can't take the place of children's company, of course, but if the children wear themselves out, they can't look after their parents well either. Now many neighbourhoods in Shanghai are developing care at home: older people stay in their own homes, and the community provides meal deliveries, home nursing and day care. There are plenty of community canteens too, where a meal costs a dozen yuan or so. For older people who can't bear to leave home, this may be a middle way. Last night, after lights out on the ward, I had a few words with a young nurse at the nurses' station. She told me her grandmother was in hospital last month back home in Hunan, and she couldn't get leave, so all she could do was video-call her every day; her grandmother always tells her not to worry, because her aunt is there. She has looked after so many other people's parents, and her own grandmother she can only see on her phone. There's no model answer to filial duty. Even if you can't be there every day, one more phone call, one more visit home, listening to them for a few more minutes: that's duty too. And for society as a whole, the question we should really be asking is: who looks after the people who look after others?
