readings.translation: Mr Chen is seventy-two. He was born in a hutong in Beijing, where he grew up, worked and married. Today he and his wife have followed their son to Shanghai, and live in an old house in a lane off Yuyuan Road. The room I rent happens to be on the first floor of that very house. As he remembers it, in the sixties his family's courtyard held five households, more than twenty people. Every morning each household lit its coal stove at the door, and the whole hutong filled with smoke. 'Back then you needed coupons for everything,' he says. 'Braised pork once a month was like New Year.' Yet in his memory, those were also the liveliest days. On summer evenings the neighbours carried bamboo chairs out into the hutong to sit in the cool, and whoever had cooked something good would always take a bowl next door. In his words: 'We were poor then, but every door was open.' In 1975, at seventeen, he was sent to the countryside, and spent three years there as an 'educated youth'. Back in Beijing, he went to work in a textile mill, on rotating shifts, and stayed twenty-two years. Meanwhile the country was changing enormously: reform and opening up, the development of Pudong, tower after tower going up. In 2000 the mill stopped production and he was laid off. He was forty-two, and his son was only six. He rarely talks about those years. It was his son who told us how, in those days, his mother knitted under the lamp every night, and his father took the jumpers out to sell by the road the next morning. At this, Mr Chen waved his hand: 'That's all in the past. Lots of us were laid off then, men and women. We all got through it the same way.' Now his son has two dumpling restaurants and is rarely home for dinner, and Duoduo, who is twelve, has four cram classes at the weekend. As he sees it, his generation 'went without everything, except time', and his son's 'has everything, except time'. As for Duoduo's generation, he laughs: 'I can't make them out, and I don't need to.' By the time the interview ended, it was dark. Mr Chen got up slowly, a hand on the table, switched on a lamp, washed his own teacup and put it back where it belonged. I couldn't help thinking that the courtyard of his childhood held five coal stoves and the voices of more than twenty people; and now, in this kitchen, three generations of one family sit round one table and listen to him alone. Looking back, I've known Mr Chen for nearly four years. I've eaten many meals that he paid for and heard him sing Beijing opera many times, but I had never seriously asked how he got to where he is. I think the most precious thing a family has isn't a new home, but people like Mr Chen, and everything they remember.

readings.translation: Every year, as soon as the dog days begin, our family group chat comes alive. 'Never use air conditioning in the dog days!' 'A glass of vinegar a day makes your blood vessels ten years younger!' 'Eat these two fruits together and you'll be poisoned!' Every one is followed by three exclamation marks, and they always start with the same words: 'Experts warn'. Chinese people set great store by looking after their health, and not just the old. Plenty of young people work late into the night while soaking goji berries in a flask, which the internet calls 'punk wellness'. Taking your health seriously is a good thing. The trouble is that there are so many claims about health that it's hard to tell true from false, and some of them can even do harm. This summer, the sentence I've heard most at my aunt's is 'I heard that...'. My uncle had just had his knees operated on, and my aunt heard bone soup was good for calcium, so she made it for him every day. But bone soup every day gives you no more calcium, just higher blood fats. Then she heard that 'a broken bone takes a hundred days', and wanted my uncle to stay in bed. But lying in bed after an operation lets the joints stiffen, and recovery is slower, not faster. In fact, a great deal of research shows that after joint surgery, the sooner you start moving under a doctor's guidance, the better you recover. So are old sayings and traditions all untrustworthy? That isn't so either. 'Early to bed, early to rise' and 'eat till you're seventy per cent full' have been shown by modern medicine to make sense. As for 'treating winter illness in summer' and dog-day plasters, some studies suggest they help some patients, but the evidence isn't strong enough yet, and the effect varies from person to person. My attitude to claims like these is: don't believe them blindly, don't dismiss them out of hand, and first ask: where's the evidence? How do you judge whether a piece of health advice is reliable? I have three simple checks. First, who's saying it: a doctor at a proper hospital, or an 'expert' selling a product? Second, is it too absolute: 'never', 'always', 'cures everything'? The bigger the claim, the more careful you should be. Third, is there research and data behind it, and not just one person's story? Finally, back to the dog days. High temperatures are most dangerous for older people and those with long-term illnesses. Air conditioning at about twenty-six degrees, plenty of water and staying in at midday will do more good than any 'secret recipe'. When it comes down to it, there's no secret to staying healthy: sleep enough, walk more, eat in moderation and stay relaxed. Everyone knows it. The hard part is doing it every day.

readings.translation: Four years ago, almost everything I knew about China came from London's Chinatown: red lanterns, sweet and sour pork, and a little restaurant called Chen Family Dumplings. If anyone had asked me then what China was like, I'd probably have said: lots of people, sweet food, and everyone very serious. Then I went to Chengdu and ate hotpot so spicy I couldn't speak; to Beijing, where I stayed a week in a hutong and listened to Chen Ming's father talk about Beijing opera all evening; to Melbourne, where I found out Chinese people had been living for more than a hundred years; and now I'm in Shanghai, living in an old house in a lane, with Chen Ming's family downstairs. Every place I've been, another label in my head has been peeled off. It turns out that behind the words 'Chinese people' are 1.4 billion different people. On this trip to Dunhuang, I saw murals more than a thousand years old in the Mogao Caves. There were flying spirits playing the pipa, and foreign merchants with big beards and pointed hats. Chen Ming's father explained to Duoduo that back then, travellers on the Silk Road carried Chinese silk and paper to the West, and brought Western music, religion and grapes into China. So cultural exchange isn't something new at all. Of course, travel can create new stereotypes too. Many people go somewhere and just take photos, tick it off and post on WeChat Moments. They only ever see the same few famous sights, and come back saying: 'I've been there. I know what it's like.' I've made that mistake myself. My first time in Beijing, I stayed five days, and wrote in my diary: 'People in Beijing all talk really fast.' In fact, I just couldn't understand them, that's all. So I've come to think more and more that what travel means doesn't lie in how many places you've been, but in whether you're willing to stop and listen to the stories of the people who live there. Broadening your horizons isn't about seeing more scenery. It's about understanding that there are so many ways to live in the world, and yours is just one of them. Chinese people often say: 'Read ten thousand books, travel ten thousand miles.' In these four years I haven't read anything like ten thousand books, but I may well have travelled ten thousand miles. Next month I'm going back to London, back to where it all began. This time, I'm taking the stories from the whole road with me.

readings.translation: This morning I bought a latte at a coffee chain in Shanghai. The same cup and the same menu can be found in Melbourne, London and Tokyo. Meanwhile, young people in London queue for bubble tea, and Melbourne supermarkets sell Sichuan hotpot base. Some say globalisation is making the world more and more alike; others say it's making it richer than ever before. First, economically, the benefits of globalisation are obvious. On the one hand, international trade makes goods cheaper and choice wider, and brings jobs to many regions; on the other, the flow of technology and knowledge lets latecomers catch up faster. Zhuxi village's baskets reaching Europe through the internet are one example. However, there's no denying that globalisation has its costs. In the global market, prices are usually set by the buyer, and small producers find it hard to bargain. To cut costs, many factories win orders at the expense of the environment and their workers' interests. And once the international situation changes, orders can vanish overnight, and those hurt most are usually the weakest. Second, culturally, the picture is more complicated. The same brands, the same films and the same pop songs are indeed making cities everywhere more and more alike. But culture doesn't only get 'assimilated'. Bubble tea in London has taken on flavours local people like; my cousin has restaurants in London and in Shanghai, and the two menus are different, but the dumplings in both are made the old Chen family way; and a Nordic homeware brand now wants to tell the story of Zhuxi's old weavers. It follows that exchange doesn't necessarily mean losing yourself; it can make both sides richer. So where does the key lie? I believe it lies in whether you can stay open while keeping what makes you distinctive. That's true of a country, and just as true of a village, a restaurant or a designer. 一格设计, where I work, is only a small studio beside Suzhou Creek, yet more than half of this year's projects have come from abroad, some from Europe and some from other countries in Asia. I've lived in three countries, and what I've learned most is this: the better you understand others, the clearer you are about who you are. In short, globalisation is neither a cure-all nor a monster. It's like a great river: it can bring a great deal, and carry a great deal away. What we can do isn't stand on the bank complaining, but learn to swim, and remember where we came from.

readings.translation: Teachers, dear friends: good afternoon! First of all, thank you to my friends at the language exchange for inviting me. One Saturday afternoon four years ago, I stood outside that door, not daring to come in. A young woman came over and asked me: 'Excuse me, are you Mark?' I was so nervous I could barely tell her my own surname. That day I learned my first words of Chinese: nǐ hǎo. Today I'd like to tell you, in Chinese, about these four years. People often ask me what's hardest about learning Chinese. My answer is: not the tones, not the characters, but keeping going. At the start I said 'sleep' for 'dumplings' and typed 'please search' for 'please find attached', made a fool of myself plenty of times, and thought about giving up. But there's an old Chinese saying: 'A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.' I had no secret. I just listened to twenty minutes of podcast on the Tube each day, wrote three sentences of diary each day, and kept going, one step at a time. Chinese has a word, 步步, 'step by step'. There are no shortcuts in learning a language: you can only go forward, step by step. So what has Chinese given me? If in the first year it gave me a few friends, then later it gave me several homes: in Chengdu, in Beijing, in Melbourne, in a lane in Shanghai. I've eaten the spiciest hotpot at the Lins', and spent New Year's Eve on the Chens' sofa. In Shanghai now, when I get back to the lane after work each day, the first thing Chen Ming's mum asks me is always: 'Have you eaten?' Chinese has taught me that 'have you eaten?' can sometimes be warmer than 'hello', and that 'take your time' may be the best encouragement in the world. More than that, Chinese has given me a new pair of eyes to see the world with. I used to think the world looked like London. Later I understood that people look at the same moon differently in Chengdu, in Melbourne and in Shanghai. Every language you learn gives you another life. Today there's a new friend here. A moment ago he was standing outside the door, not daring to come in, exactly as I was four years ago. My new friend, I want to say to you: don't be afraid of getting it wrong, because that's how you remember; don't do it by halves, and don't give up halfway. One day you'll find that every step you've taken counts. Finally, I'd like to thank Xiaoyu, my first Chinese teacher and my best friend; Chen Ming, who has fed me dumplings for four years and laughed at my lateness for just as long; his mum and dad, who have treated me as one of their own; Duoduo, who remembers every tone I've got wrong in four years; and this café too. Confucius said: 'Is it not a joy to have friends come from afar?' Today Chen Ming's family have flown back from Shanghai, and friends have come here from every corner of London, and I really am very happy. There's no end to learning, and I still have a lot of Chinese to learn. But I'm not afraid any more. Thank you, everyone!

q.text: 马克今天几点到的？陈明为什么说“太阳真从西边出来了”？
options: 他六点半就到了，比约的时间早了半个小时。因为马克以前总是迟到，四年前的中秋也迟到了。
因为马克把“始于足下”的“于”说成了第三声，其实应该是第二声。
她做了西红柿炒鸡蛋。陈明教给了马克，马克又教给了她。

drills.pinyin: zhège miànbāo shì wǒ zìjǐ kǎo de.
drills.en: I baked this bread myself.
Do you like potatoes?
Let's have roast chicken on Sunday.
The roast potatoes are so tasty!
I'll wash the potatoes first.

drills.pinyin: yīfu xǐ le ma? hái méi xǐ.
drills.en: Have you washed the clothes? Not yet.

drills.pinyin: nǐ qiē de tài kuài le, xiǎoxīn!
drills.en: You're chopping too fast, careful!
Cut the potatoes a bit smaller.

drills.pinyin: nǐ zuòfàn, wǒ bāng máng xǐ wǎn.
drills.en: You cook, and I'll help with the washing-up.

drills.hanzi: 今天谁洗碗？要我帮忙吗？
drills.pinyin: jīntiān shéi xǐ wǎn? yào wǒ bāng máng ma?
drills.en: Who's washing up today? Do you want a hand?

drills.pinyin: zhège cài hěn jiǎndān, wǒ jiāo nǐ.
drills.en: This dish is simple, I'll teach you.
Actually, cooking is easy.
Duoduo is getting taller and taller!

drills.hanzi: 天气越来越暖和，我们去公园吧。
drills.pinyin: tiānqì yuèláiyuè nuǎnhuo, wǒmen qù gōngyuán ba.
drills.en: It's getting warmer and warmer, let's go to the park.
I hope it's sunny tomorrow.

drills.hanzi: 我希望新家的厨房大一点儿。
drills.pinyin: wǒ xīwàng xīn jiā de chúfáng dà yīdiǎnr.
drills.en: I hope the kitchen in the new flat is a bit bigger.

drills.pinyin: yán zài nǎr? zài guō pángbiān.
drills.en: Where's the salt? Next to the wok.
Don't put in too much salt!

drills.hanzi: 这个锅太小了，厨房里还有大的吗？
drills.pinyin: zhège guō tài xiǎo le, chúfáng lǐ hái yǒu dà de ma?
drills.en: This wok is too small. Is there a bigger one in the kitchen?
Careful, the knife is sharp!

drills.pinyin: nǐ yǒu dāo ma? wǒ yào qiē miànbāo.
drills.en: Have you got a knife? I need to cut the bread.

drills.pinyin: nǐ chī guo Běijīng kǎoyā ma?
drills.en: Have you ever had Peking roast duck?

drills.hanzi: 我们吃烤鸭吧，甜点我来做。
drills.pinyin: wǒmen chī kǎoyā ba, tiándiǎn wǒ lái zuò.
drills.en: Let's have roast duck, and I'll make dessert.

drills.pinyin: bīngxiāng lǐ hái yǒu píjiǔ ma?
drills.en: Is there any beer left in the fridge?
Use a bit less oil.
This dish is too oily.

drills.hanzi: 这些是你的，那些是我的。
drills.pinyin: zhèxiē shì nǐ de, nàxiē shì wǒ de.
drills.en: These are yours, those are mine.

drills.pinyin: nàxiē shuǐguǒ fàng bīngxiāng lǐ ba.
drills.en: Put that fruit in the fridge.

drills.hanzi: 我没听清楚，请再说一遍。
drills.en: I didn't catch that clearly. Could you say it again?

drills.pinyin: zhèxiē nǐ dōu tīng qīngchu le ma?
drills.en: Did you hear all of these clearly?

drills.hanzi: 你的中文进步了很多！哪里哪里，还差得远呢。
drills.pinyin: nǐ de zhōngwén jìnbù le hěnduō! nǎlǐnǎlǐ, hái chàdeyuǎn ne.
drills.en: Your Chinese has improved a lot! Oh, not really, I've still got a long way to go.
He's making really fast progress.

drills.pinyin: kèrén dōu dào le ma? lái, gānbēi!
drills.en: Have all the guests arrived? Come on, cheers!

drills.pinyin: kèrén dōu juéde wèidao hěn hǎo.
drills.en: The guests all thought it tasted great.
How does this soup taste?

drills.hanzi: 汤有点儿淡，再放点儿盐吧。
drills.pinyin: tāng yǒudiǎnr dàn, zài fàng diǎnr yán ba.
drills.en: The soup is a bit bland, put a bit more salt in.

drills.pinyin: zhège cài tài dàn le, zhēn nán chī.
drills.en: This dish is far too bland. It's horrible.

drills.hanzi: 我希望明年能说流利的中文。
drills.pinyin: wǒ xīwàng míngnián néng shuō liúlì de zhōngwén.
drills.en: I hope I can speak fluent Chinese next year.

drills.hanzi: 她学得很认真，现在说得很流利。
drills.pinyin: tā xué de hěn rènzhēn, xiànzài shuō de hěn liúlì.
drills.en: She studied hard, and now she speaks fluently.
Duoduo is so clever!

drills.hanzi: 他很聪明，工作也很认真。
drills.pinyin: tā hěn cōngming, gōngzuò yě hěn rènzhēn.
drills.en: He's clever, and he's very conscientious at work too.
Run! The bus is coming!

drills.pinyin: tā pǎo de bǐ wǒ kuài.
drills.en: He runs faster than me.

drills.hanzi: 你的发音很好，口语也不错。
drills.pinyin: nǐ de fāyīn hěn hǎo, kǒuyǔ yě bùcuò.
drills.en: Your pronunciation is very good, and your speaking is good too.
I practise speaking every day.

drills.hanzi: 他的中文水平越来越高了。
drills.pinyin: tā de zhōngwén shuǐpíng yuèláiyuè gāo le.
drills.en: His level of Chinese is getting higher and higher.

drills.pinyin: lǎoshī kuā wǒ de fāyīn le!
drills.en: The teacher praised my pronunciation!

drills.hanzi: 别夸我了，我的水平还差得远呢！
drills.pinyin: bié kuā wǒ le, wǒ de shuǐpíng hái chàdeyuǎn ne!
drills.en: Stop praising me, my level is still a long way off!
Is the railway station far from here?

drills.hanzi: 我刚到火车站，你在哪儿？
drills.pinyin: wǒ gāng dào huǒchēzhàn, nǐ zài nǎr?
drills.en: I've just got to the station. Where are you?
Sorry, I overslept!
He's just gone out.

drills.hanzi: 又起晚了？你没有闹钟吗？
drills.pinyin: yòu qǐwǎn le? nǐ méiyǒu nàozhōng ma?
drills.en: Overslept again? Don't you have an alarm clock?
My alarm clock is broken.
I didn't wake up until ten.
Why are you only coming now?

drills.pinyin: Duǒduo yī xǐng jiù yào chī zǎofàn.
drills.en: As soon as Duoduo wakes up, she wants breakfast.

drills.hanzi: 我们等了半天，公交车才来。
drills.pinyin: wǒmen děng le bàn tiān, gōngjiāochē cái lái.
drills.en: We waited ages before the bus came.
Let's go, we're running out of time!
He definitely isn't up yet.
If we go now, we definitely won't make it.
If we leave now, will we still make it?
There are still ten minutes. We'll make it.

drills.pinyin: xià yī bān jǐ diǎn? shí diǎn yī kè.
drills.en: When's the next one? Quarter past ten.

drills.hanzi: 最后一班的车票还有吗？
drills.pinyin: zuìhòu yī bān de chēpiào hái yǒu ma?
drills.en: Are there still tickets for the last train?

drills.hanzi: 去剑桥的火车在几号站台？
drills.pinyin: qù Jiànqiáo de huǒchē zài jǐ hào zhàntái?
drills.en: Which platform is the train to Cambridge on?

drills.hanzi: 我早就到站台了，你在哪儿？
drills.pinyin: wǒ zǎojiù dào zhàntái le, nǐ zài nǎr?
drills.en: I got to the platform ages ago. Where are you?
Is this seat taken?
Where are our seats?
I've got a train to catch, bye!
No need to rush, there's still time.
He's always on time for work.

drills.hanzi: 明天我请假，我们早上八点准时出发！
drills.pinyin: míngtiān wǒ qǐngjià, wǒmen zǎoshang bā diǎn zhǔnshí chūfā!
drills.en: I'm taking tomorrow off. We'll set off at eight sharp!

drills.hanzi: 你请假了吗？我们几点出发？
drills.pinyin: nǐ qǐngjià le ma? wǒmen jǐ diǎn chūfā?
drills.en: Have you got the day off? What time do we set off?

drills.pinyin: dà hòu tiān wǒ yào qǐngjià.
drills.en: I'm taking the day off in three days' time.

drills.pinyin: lùshang dǔchē, wǒ wǎn diǎn'ér dào.
drills.en: There's traffic on the way, so I'll be a bit late.
Stuck in traffic? Don't worry.

drills.hanzi: 她平常不喝咖啡，今天喝了两杯！
drills.pinyin: tā píngcháng bù hē kāfēi, jīntiān hē le liǎng bēi!
drills.en: She doesn't usually drink coffee, but today she had two cups!
What time do you usually get up?

drills.hanzi: 时刻表我看了半天，也没看懂。
drills.pinyin: shíkèbiǎo wǒ kàn le bàntiān, yě méi kàn dǒng.
drills.en: I looked at the timetable for ages and still couldn't make sense of it.

drills.hanzi: 你别着急，我们看一下时刻表。
drills.pinyin: nǐ bié zháojí, wǒmen kàn yīxià shíkèbiǎo.
drills.en: Don't worry, let's look at the timetable.

drills.hanzi: 这个太大了，能换一个吗？
drills.pinyin: zhège tài dà le, néng huàn yī gè ma?
drills.en: This one's too big. Can I swap it?

drills.hanzi: 上上个星期我换了新手机。
drills.pinyin: shàngshànggexīngqī wǒ huàn le xīn shǒujī.
drills.en: I got a new phone the week before last.

drills.hanzi: 你准时到了？太阳从西边出来了！
drills.pinyin: nǐ zhǔnshí dào le? tàiyáng cóng xībiān chūlai le!
drills.en: You're on time? Pigs might fly!
Is the park on the west side or the east side?
The Tube station is on the east side. It isn't far.
The sun has finally come out!

drills.pinyin: nǐ chūlai yīxià, wǒ zài ménkǒu.
drills.en: Come out for a minute, I'm at the door.
We've finally got to Cambridge!
What are you planning to do in the summer holidays?

drills.pinyin: shǔjià wǒ zài jiā dāi liǎng gè yuè.
drills.en: I'm staying at home for two months over the summer holidays.

drills.hanzi: 你在伦敦待到几月？七月底。
drills.pinyin: nǐ zài Lúndūn dài dào jǐ yuè? qī yuè dǐ.
drills.en: Until which month are you staying in London? Until the end of July.

drills.pinyin: zhège yuè dǐ wǒ hěn máng.
drills.en: I'm very busy at the end of this month.
Have you read the email?

drills.pinyin: wǎnshang wǒ gěi nǐ xiě yóujiàn.
drills.en: I'll write you an email this evening.

drills.pinyin: shíjiān gǎi le, qī diǎn kāishǐ.
drills.en: The time has changed. It starts at seven.
I keep a diary in Chinese.

drills.hanzi: 我的日记你帮我改一下，好吗？
drills.pinyin: wǒ de rìjì nǐ bāng wǒ gǎi yīxià, hǎo ma?
drills.en: Could you correct my diary for me?
Leave a bit for me!

drills.pinyin: wǒ gěi nǐ liú le yī kuài dàngāo.
drills.en: I've saved you a piece of cake.

drills.hanzi: 你的作业写了吗？还没写。
drills.pinyin: nǐ de zuòyè xiě le ma? hái méi xiě.
drills.en: Have you done your homework? Not yet.

drills.hanzi: 朵朵每天都有很多作业。
drills.pinyin: Duǒduo měitiān dōu yǒu hěnduō zuòyè.
drills.en: Duoduo has lots of homework every day.
When do you break up for the holidays?

drills.pinyin: xià gè xīngqī jiù fàngjià le!
drills.en: We break up next week!

drills.hanzi: 这个学期太忙了，下个学期好一点儿。
drills.pinyin: zhège xuéqī tài máng le, xià gè xuéqī hǎo yīdiǎnr.
drills.en: This term is too busy. Next term will be a bit better.

drills.hanzi: 我给她写了信，她还没回信。
drills.pinyin: wǒ gěi tā xiě le xìn, tā hái méi huíxìn.
drills.en: I wrote her a letter, but she hasn't written back yet.
She wrote back to me!

drills.pinyin: wǒ gěi nǐ jì le yī běn shū.
drills.en: I've posted you a book.
How long does it take to post it to Chengdu?
What's your address?

drills.pinyin: nǐ jiā de dìzhǐ fā gěi wǒ ba.
drills.en: Send me your home address.

drills.pinyin: qīn'ài de, wǒmen dǎ shìpín ba!
drills.en: Darling, let's do a video call!

drills.hanzi: 亲爱的妈妈，你最近好吗？
drills.pinyin: qīn'ài de māma, nǐ zuìjìn hǎo ma?
drills.en: Dear Mum, how have you been?

drills.hanzi: 最近我常常跟她打视频。
drills.pinyin: zuìjìn wǒ chángcháng gēn tā dǎ shìpín.
drills.en: I often video-call her these days.
Dear Duoduo, happy birthday!

drills.hanzi: 亲爱的，别难过，我们九月见！
drills.pinyin: qīn'ài de, bié nán guò, wǒmen jiǔ yuè jiàn!
drills.en: Darling, don't be sad, we'll see each other in September!
I'll pick you up at the airport.

drills.pinyin: zài jīchǎng, dàjiā dōu hěn nánguò.
drills.en: At the airport, everyone was sad.

drills.pinyin: zhè piān rìjì xiě de zhēn hǎo!
drills.en: This diary entry is really well written!
How many Chinese characters can you write?

drills.hanzi: 我每天写一篇日记，练习汉字。
drills.pinyin: wǒ měitiān xiě yī piān rìjì, liànxí hànzì.
drills.en: I write a diary entry every day to practise characters.

drills.hanzi: 我想了很久，还是决定去。
drills.pinyin: wǒ xiǎng le hěn jiǔ, háishi juédìng qù.
drills.en: I thought about it for a long time, and I still decided to go.
Have you decided?

drills.pinyin: hǎo jiǔ bù jiàn, nǐ shòu le!
drills.en: Long time no see, you've lost weight!

drills.pinyin: zhè fēng xìn shì shéi xiě de?
drills.en: Who wrote this letter?

drills.hanzi: 他给我写了一封很长的邮件。
drills.pinyin: tā gěi wǒ xiě le yī fēng hěn cháng de yóujiàn.
drills.en: He wrote me a really long email.
Wishing you good health!

drills.hanzi: 好久不见！行李箱重吗？我帮你拿。
drills.pinyin: hǎojiǔbùjiàn! xínglixiāng zhòng ma? wǒ bāng nǐ ná.
drills.en: Long time no see! Is your suitcase heavy? I'll carry it for you.
I'll take the suitcase in.
It's cold outside, let's go in.

drills.pinyin: tā zǒu le, wǒ xīnli hěn nánguò.
drills.en: She's gone, and I feel really sad inside.

drills.hanzi: 听到你身体健康，我心里很高兴。
drills.pinyin: tīngdào nǐ shēntǐ jiànkāng, wǒ xīnli hěn gāoxìng.
drills.en: I'm really glad to hear you're in good health.

drills.pinyin: nǐ shōudào wǒ de yóujiàn le ma?
drills.en: Did you get my email?
I got the present, thanks!
Wait a moment, I'm coming right away!

drills.pinyin: wǒ zài wǎngshang mǎi le jīpiào.
drills.en: I bought my plane ticket online.

drills.hanzi: 网上的机票便宜一点儿。
drills.en: Plane tickets are a bit cheaper online.
Chengdu hotpot is really spicy.

drills.pinyin: wǒmen mǎshàng qù chī huǒguō ba!
drills.en: Let's go for hotpot right now!

drills.pinyin: wǒ xiǎng qù Chéngdū kàn xióngmāo.
drills.en: I want to go to Chengdu to see the pandas.
Duoduo loves pandas most of all.
We had a great time today!
Why aren't you happy today?
Have you brought your passport?
Do you need a visa to go to China?

drills.hanzi: 签证和护照都在我这儿。
drills.pinyin: qiānzhèng hé hùzhào dōu zài wǒ zhèr.
drills.en: I've got both the visa and the passport.

drills.pinyin: zhè cì lǚxíng tài kāixīn le!
drills.en: This trip was so much fun!

drills.pinyin: wǒ xiǎng qù hěnduō chéngshì lǚxíng.
drills.en: I want to travel to lots of cities.
Which city do you like best?

drills.pinyin: fàngxīn, wǒ huì zhàogù tā de.
drills.en: Don't worry, I'll look after her.

drills.pinyin: xièxie nǐ zhè jǐ tiān zhàogù wǒ!
drills.en: Thank you for looking after me these last few days!
The supermarket doesn't open until nine.
Please open the door! It's Mark.
The restaurant is closed on Mondays.

drills.pinyin: kuài guānmén le, wǒmen zǒu ba.
drills.en: It's about to close, let's go.
Where's your hometown?
My family comes from Sichuan.

drills.pinyin: gěi wǒ jì yī zhāng míngxìnpiàn ba!
drills.en: Send me a postcard!

drills.hanzi: 我收到了你的明信片，太开心了！
drills.pinyin: wǒ shōudào le nǐ de míngxìnpiàn, tài kāixīn le!
drills.en: I got your postcard, and I'm so happy!

drills.hanzi: 一路平安！到了给我发微信。
drills.pinyin: yīlùpíng'ān! dào le gěi wǒ fā wēixìn.
drills.en: Have a safe journey! Message me when you get there.

drills.hanzi: 朵朵一边哭一边说：“一路平安！”
drills.pinyin: Duǒduo yībiān kū yībiān shuō: yīlùpíng'ān!
drills.en: Duoduo cried as she wished her a safe journey.

drills.hanzi: 别哭了，她九月就回来了。
drills.pinyin: bié kū le, tā jiǔ yuè jiù huí lai le.
drills.en: Stop crying, she'll be back in September.
